RT @fedesarquis: You can try the prompt yourself! Here:

Create a seamless 4–5-second looping GIF celebrating [BRAND NAM
viral_ticker_tweets.title_en:
RT @fedesarquis: You can try the prompt yourself! Here:

Create a seamless 4–5-second looping GIF celebrating [BRAND NAME], using the attached logo as the exact shape reference.

Center the logo on a near-black navy background. Rebuild it entirely from visible ASCII characters: @ # % * + = 0 1. Preserve its proportions, silhouette, and negative space. Keep the shape stable while the characters continuously shuffle.

Animate [BRAND COLORS] through the ASCII logo, accented by golden-yellow light. A brilliant white-gold highlight sweeps across the characters, creating a luminous bloom while keeping individual glyphs readable.

Surround it with electric-cyan and brand-colored ASCII characters flowing in an orbital trail. Add dramatic sparkling light: large four- and eight-point starbursts that flare and fade, smaller twinkling + characters, and occasional bright glints along the logo’s edges.

Beneath the logo, display “[BRAND NAME OR PRODUCT NAME]” in a crisp, stationary monospace font.

Square composition, smooth motion, seamless loop. Radiant retro-terminal aesthetic, strong contrast, generous breathing room. The developer’s logo is the unmistakable hero.

viral_ticker_tweets.title:
Traditional transcription software could be one of the first categories AI makes almost unnecessary.

Think about tools
viral_ticker_tweets.title_en:
Traditional transcription software could be one of the first categories AI makes almost unnecessary.

Think about tools like Otter or other platforms built mainly to convert speech into text, identify speakers, summarize meetings, and organize notes.

AI can already perform most of these tasks without requiring users to move between different applications.

But the  bigger threat goes beyond transcription.

AI is changing how people interact with software. Instead of opening five different tools to complete one task, you could simply give an AI agent an instruction and let it handle the entire process.

Software companies built businesses around individual tasks. AI is increasingly combining those tasks into one system.
viral_ticker_tweets.title_zh:

One thing I think matters a lot with autonomous AI agents is not just what they can do, but what
viral_ticker_tweets.title_en:
Top of the Morning CT

One thing I think matters a lot with autonomous AI agents is not just what they can do, but what they are allowed to do.

That is where @meetmotes gets interesting.

Motes gives each AI agent its own identity and smart account, but the owner can define the boundaries around that autonomy.

You can set things like:

→ Which assets the agent can use
→ How much it can trade
→ Daily spending or execution limits
→ Slippage conditions
→ When actions should require more control

That creates a different model from simply handing an AI agent access to your wallet and hoping it makes good decisions.

The agent can operate within predefined rules, while the user keeps control over the authority behind those actions.

And I think the most important part may be what happens when conditions change.

A useful autonomous agent shouldn't always be trying to execute.

Sometimes the correct action is to pause, reassess the situation, or ask the owner for approval before continuing.

That balance between automation and restraint is what could make agentic finance more practical.

The bigger question for Motes is whether these permissioned agents can prove they are reliable enough for users to trust them with increasingly valuable onchain activity.

Autonomy is useful.

Bounded autonomy is what makes it usable.

viral_ticker_tweets.quote_zh:
早间 CT 顶部

我认为对于自主人工智能代理来说，最重要的一件事不仅在于它们可以做什么，还在于它们被允许做什么。

这就是@meetmotes 有趣的地方。

Motes 为每个人工智能代理提供了自己的身份和智能帐户，但所有者可以定义该自治权的边界。

您可以设置如下内容：

→ 代理可以使用哪些资产
→ 可以交易多少
→ 每日支出或执行限额
→ 滑移条件
→ 当行动需要更多控制时

这创建了一个不同的模型，与简单地让人工智能代理访问你的钱包并希望它做出正确的决策不同。

代理可以在预定义的规则内操作，而用户则可以控制这些操作背后的权限。

我认为最重要的部分可能是当条件发生变化时会发生什么。

一个有用的自主代理不应该总是试图执行。

有时，正确的行动是暂停，重新评估情况，或在继续之前征求所有者的批准。

自动化和约束之间的平衡可以使代理金融更加实用。

Motes 面临的更大问题是，这些获得许可的代理是否能够证明它们足够可靠，让用户信任它们进行越来越有价值的链上活动。

自治是有用的。

有限的自主权使其可用。

The interesting part of @meetmotes is not just the NFT artwork. It's the architecture behind each Mot
viral_ticker_tweets.title_en:
Good morning, CT.

The interesting part of @meetmotes is not just the NFT artwork. It's the architecture behind each Mote.

Think of it as three connected layers:

1. The NFT: Identity
Each Mote NFT represents an agent identity. It is the ownership reference, not where the funds are stored.

2. The agent: Intelligence
The agent service proposes actions based on the owner's chosen strategy and permissions.

3. The smart account: Control
This is where the assets are held. It enforces the owner's rules, including approved actions, spending limits and other permission boundaries.

The owner remains in control of what the agent is allowed to do.

That's what makes the model interesting: one NFT-linked agent identity, one dedicated smart account and permissions defined by the owner.

Eligible agent activity can also generate protocol fees, connecting actual usage to the wider Motes ecosystem.

The artwork gives each Mote its public identity. The architecture gives that identity a purpose.

More than an NFT collection, it's an attempt to make digital ownership useful in an agent-driven economy.

viral_ticker_tweets.title_en:
‼️Nick Shirley CAUGHT Lying About Being In New York The Day Charlie  Was ASSASSINATED — And It BLOWS UP Andrew Kolvet's Only Alibi 😱

Nick Shirley was NOT in New York City on September 10th. He was in Utah. A video he posted from the Orem train station that same day catches the ticket agent announcing the location over the PA system in the background — the audio places him minutes from where Charlie Kirk was shot. The next day, September 11th, he films himself at Salt Lake City International Airport, and the scenery outside the window matches public photos of that terminal exactly.

Two clips. Two days. Same state.

That single fact destroys the story he has repeated: that he had already gone back to New York, and that the segment he did with Andrew Kolvet on The Charlie Kirk Show that morning was live. If Nick was standing in Utah on the 10th and again on the 11th, the interview could not have been live. And if it was not live, the one real-time alibi Andrew Kolvet has ever offered for his own movements that morning evaporates.

It gets worse. Nick says Charlie texted him the night of the 9th inviting him onto the show on Thursday the 11th — and that he had originally planned to livestream the UVU event in person before "last-minute obligations" forced him to New York. But Charlie himself was scheduled to be at Charis Bible College in Colorado on the 11th. So why is Charlie trying to book Nick for an interview on a day Charlie already had somewhere else to be? And why does the screenshot Nick released show only a partial thread, cut off exactly where the useful part of the conversation would be?

Then there is the part almost nobody has clocked. In that September 10th train station video, Nick is already pushing the fed-slop line — radical leftists, Antifa, blame the left — before a single fact about the shooter or the motive was public. Not hours later. Not after a briefing. On the day, on camera, before the evidence existed.

Put it together and it stops looking like a coincidence. It looks like Nick Shirley was inserted into the Charlie Kirk timeline to sell the official story to Gen Z before anyone could check it, and to help manufacture an alibi for Andrew Kolvet while he was at it. That is not organic journalism. That is a jacketed asset doing precisely what it was placed there to do.

And here is your update: Nick Shirley says this is all false. So I asked him for the originals of the photos he claims debunk me, so the metadata could be verified. He refused.

He has the files. He has the timestamps. He will not hand them over. You tell me what that means.

Nick Shirley's public answer to all of this is that it's false. Fine. Good. That is exactly what a correction is for — so I went to him privately and asked for the one thing that settles it either way: the original uncompressed files, so the metadata could be checked by someone who actually knows what he's looking at.

Here is what happened.

He opened with confidence: "Yes 100% I filmed it at JFK before I went to the UK." I told him if it checks out, I will apologize and correct the record publicly. He replied, "Yes a correction deserves to be served."

So I asked for the files. Original, uncompressed, straight from the camera roll — WeTransfer, Dropbox, anything, to an email address. Nothing exotic. Just the files.

What came back was a screenshot of the Photos app. A screen recording of a video player. Four photos pasted into the chat. And one file preview captioned "John F. Kennedy International… September 11, 2025 9:39 PM."

Every one of those is a copy of a copy. Re-saved, re-compressed, stripped. A screenshot of a screenshot carries no camera metadata at all. It carries whatever the phone decided to write on the label — which is precisely the thing under dispute. So he has handed me the claim again, not the evidence for it.

And here is where his own defense starts to break. His version is now: "I had an office in NYC that I lived in at that time and was in NYC by Sept 7 and then left for the UK on the 12th." Except there is a clip of him at the Orem train station on the 10th, with the ticket agent calling out the location over the PA. So which is it — New York from the 7th, or Utah on the 10th? Both cannot be true without a same-day cross-country round trip that nobody has produced a boarding pass for.

Look at the airport clip he sent as proof. The label on the file says JFK, 9:39 PM on September 11th. The scenery outside that window is Salt Lake City. He is using a file tagged one airport to prove he was at the other.

He says the timeline is wrong. He has the originals. He will not send them. "A correction deserves to be served" — then serve it.

A screenshot is not metadata. A label is not a timestamp. And a guy who is this confident should not be this hard to get a file out of.

CC: @AndrewKolvet

两个剪辑。两天。相同的状态。

这个事实摧毁了他重复的故事：他已经回到了纽约，而且那天早上他在《查理·柯克秀》上与安德鲁·科尔维特一起做的片段正在直播。如果尼克10日和11日再次站在犹他州，采访就不可能进行现场直播。如果不是现场直播，安德鲁·科尔维特为自己那天早上的行动提供的实时不在场证据就会消失。

情况变得更糟。尼克说，查理在 9 日晚上给他发短信，邀请他参加 11 日星期四的节目，他原本计划亲自直播 UVU 活动，但“最后一刻的义务”迫使他前往纽约。但查理本人原定于11日前往科罗拉多州的查理斯圣经学院。那么为什么查理要在查理已经有其他地方可去的日子里试图预订尼克接受采访呢？为什么尼克发布的截图只显示了部分线索，准确地切断了对话中有用的部分？

然后是几乎没有人打卡的部分。在 9 月 10 日的火车站视频中，在有关枪手或动机的单一事实公开之前，尼克就已经在推行美联储的路线了——激进左翼分子、安提法（Antifa）指责左翼。不到几个小时后。不是在通报之后。那天，在证据出现之前，镜头前。

把它们放在一起，它看起来就不再是巧合了。尼克·雪莉（Nick Shirley）似乎被插入查理·柯克（Charlie Kirk）的时间线，以便在任何人都可以检查之前将官方故事出售给 Z 世代，并在安德鲁·科尔维特（Andrew Kolvet）参与其中时帮助他制造不在场证明。那不是有机新闻。这是一个被夹套的资产，它的作用正是它被放置在那里的目的。

这是您的更新：尼克·雪莉说这都是假的。所以我向他索要他声称揭穿我的照片的原件，以便可以验证元数据。他拒绝了。

他有文件。他有时间戳。他不会把它们交出来。你告诉我这意味着什么。

尼克·雪莉对这一切的公开回答是，这是错误的。美好的。好的。这正是修正的目的——所以我私下去找他，要求提供一件事来解决这个问题：原始的未压缩文件，这样元数据就可以由真正知道他在看什么的人检查。

这就是发生的事情。

他自信地开口说道：“是的，100%是我在去英国之前在肯尼迪机场拍摄的。”我告诉他，如果结果属实，我会公开道歉并更正记录。他回答说：“是的，值得更正。”

所以我索要了文件。原始、未压缩、直接从相机胶卷 - WeTransfer、Dropbox、任何东西，到电子邮件地址。没什么异国情调。只是文件。

返回的是照片应用程序的屏幕截图。视频播放器的屏幕录制。聊天中粘贴了四张照片。一份文件预览标题为“约翰·肯尼迪国际……2025 年 9 月 11 日晚上 9:39”。

其中每一个都是副本的副本。重新保存、重新压缩、剥离。屏幕截图的屏幕截图根本不包含相机元数据。它带有手机决定在标签上写的任何内容——这正是有争议的内容。所以他又给了我这个主张，而不是证据。

这就是他自己的防御开始崩溃的地方。他现在的版本是：“我当时住在纽约市有一个办公室，9月7日到达纽约，然后于12日前往英国。”不过有一段他10日在奥勒姆火车站的视频，售票员通过扩音器喊出位置。那么是哪一个——7号的纽约，还是10号的犹他州？如果没有当天的跨国往返旅行，而且没有人出示登机牌，这两种情况都不可能成立。

看看他发送的机场剪辑作为证据。文件上的标签写着“肯尼迪国际机场”，9 月 11 日晚上 9:39。窗外的风景就是盐湖城。他正在使用标记一个机场的文件来证明他去过另一个机场。

他说时间表是错误的。他有原件。他不会派他们去。 “应该进行更正”——然后就可以了。

屏幕截图不是元数据。标签不是时间戳。一个如此自信的人应该不会那么难拿到文件。

这个事实摧毁了他重复的故事：他已经回到了纽约，而且那天早上他在《查理·柯克秀》上与安德鲁·科尔维特一起做的片段正在直播。如果尼克10日和11日再次站在犹他州，采访就不可能进行现场直播。如果不是现场直播，安德鲁·科尔维特为自己那天早上的行动提供的实时不在场证据就会消失。

情况变得更糟。尼克说，查理在 9 日晚上给他发短信，邀请他参加 11 日星期四的节目，他原本计划亲自直播 UVU 活动，但“最后一刻的义务”迫使他前往纽约。但查理本人原定于11日前往科罗拉多州的查理斯圣经学院。那么为什么查理要在查理已经有其他地方可去的日子里试图预订尼克接受采访呢？为什么尼克发布的截图只显示了部分线索，准确地切断了对话中有用的部分？

然后是几乎没有人打卡的部分。在 9 月 10 日的火车站视频中，在有关枪手或动机的单一事实公开之前，尼克就已经在推行美联储的路线了——激进左翼分子、安提法（Antifa）指责左翼。不到几个小时后。不是在通报之后。那天，在证据出现之前，镜头前。

把它们放在一起，它看起来就不再是巧合了。尼克·雪莉（Nick Shirley）似乎被插入查理·柯克（Charlie Kirk）的时间线，以便在任何人都可以检查之前将官方故事出售给 Z 世代，并在安德鲁·科尔维特（Andrew Kolvet）参与其中时帮助他制造不在场证明。那不是有机新闻。这是一个被夹套的资产，它的作用正是它被放置在那里的目的。

这是您的更新：尼克·雪莉说这都是假的。所以我向他索要他声称揭穿我的照片的原件，以便可以验证元数据。他拒绝了。

他有文件。他有时间戳。他不会把它们交出来。你告诉我这意味着什么。

尼克·雪莉对这一切的公开回答是，这是错误的。美好的。好的。这正是修正的目的——所以我私下去找他，要求提供一件事来解决这个问题：原始的未压缩文件，这样元数据就可以由真正知道他在看什么的人检查。

这就是发生的事情。

他自信地开口说道：“是的，100%是我在去英国之前在肯尼迪机场拍摄的。”我告诉他，如果结果属实，我会公开道歉并更正记录。他回答说：“是的，值得更正。”

所以我索要了文件。原始、未压缩、直接从相机胶卷 - WeTransfer、Dropbox、任何东西，到电子邮件地址。没什么异国情调。只是文件。

返回的是照片应用程序的屏幕截图。视频播放器的屏幕录制。聊天中粘贴了四张照片。一份文件预览标题为“约翰·肯尼迪国际……2025 年 9 月 11 日晚上 9:39”。

其中每一个都是副本的副本。重新保存、重新压缩、剥离。屏幕截图的屏幕截图根本不包含相机元数据。它带有手机决定在标签上写的任何内容——这正是有争议的内容。所以他又给了我这个主张，而不是证据。

这就是他自己的防御开始崩溃的地方。他现在的版本是：“我当时住在纽约市有一个办公室，9月7日到达纽约，然后于12日前往英国。”不过有一段他10日在奥勒姆火车站的视频，售票员通过扩音器喊出位置。那么是哪一个——7号的纽约，还是10号的犹他州？如果没有当天的跨国往返旅行，而且没有人出示登机牌，这两种情况都不可能成立。

看看他发送的机场剪辑作为证据。文件上的标签写着“肯尼迪国际机场”，9 月 11 日晚上 9:39。窗外的风景就是盐湖城。他正在使用标记一个机场的文件来证明他去过另一个机场。

他说时间表是错误的。他有原件。他不会派他们去。 “应该进行更正”——然后就可以了。

屏幕截图不是元数据。标签不是时间戳。一个如此自信的人应该不会那么难拿到文件。

viral_ticker_tweets.content_snippet:
‼️Nick Shirley CAUGHT Lying About Being In New York The Day Charlie  Was ASSASSINATED — And It BLOWS UP Andrew Kolvet's Only Alibi 😱

Nick Shirley was NOT in New York City on September 10th. He was in Utah. A video he posted from the Orem train station that same day catches the ticket agent announcing the location over the PA system in the background — the audio places him minutes from where Charlie Kirk was shot. The next day, September 11th, he films himself at Salt Lake City International Airport, and the scenery outside the window matches public photos of that terminal exactly.

Two clips. Two days. Same state.

That single fact destroys the story he has repeated: that he had already gone back to New York, and that the segment he did with Andrew Kolvet on The Charlie Kirk Show that morning was live. If Nick was standing in Utah on the 10th and again on the 11th, the interview could not have been live. And if it was not live, the one real-time alibi Andrew Kolvet has ever offered for his own movements that morning evaporates.

It gets worse. Nick says Charlie texted him the night of the 9th inviting him onto the show on Thursday the 11th — and that he had originally planned to livestream the UVU event in person before "last-minute obligations" forced him to New York. But Charlie himself was scheduled to be at Charis Bible College in Colorado on the 11th. So why is Charlie trying to book Nick for an interview on a day Charlie already had somewhere else to be? And why does the screenshot Nick released show only a partial thread, cut off exactly where the useful part of the conversation would be?

Then there is the part almost nobody has clocked. In that September 10th train station video, Nick is already pushing the fed-slop line — radical leftists, Antifa, blame the left — before a single fact about the shooter or the motive was public. Not hours later. Not after a briefing. On the day, on camera, before the evidence existed.

Put it together and it stops looking like a coincidence. It looks like Nick Shirley was inserted into the Charlie Kirk timeline to sell the official story to Gen Z before anyone could check it, and to help manufacture an alibi for Andrew Kolvet while he was at it. That is not organic journalism. That is a jacketed asset doing precisely what it was placed there to do.

And here is your update: Nick Shirley says this is all false. So I asked him for the originals of the photos he claims debunk me, so the metadata could be verified. He refused.

He has the files. He has the timestamps. He will not hand them over. You tell me what that means.

Nick Shirley's public answer to all of this is that it's false. Fine. Good. That is exactly what a correction is for — so I went to him privately and asked for the one thing that settles it either way: the original uncompressed files, so the metadata could be checked by someone who actually knows what he's looking at.

Here is what happened.

He opened with confidence: "Yes 100% I filmed it at JFK before I went to the UK." I told him if it checks out, I will apologize and correct the record publicly. He replied, "Yes a correction deserves to be served."

So I asked for the files. Original, uncompressed, straight from the camera roll — WeTransfer, Dropbox, anything, to an email address. Nothing exotic. Just the files.

What came back was a screenshot of the Photos app. A screen recording of a video player. Four photos pasted into the chat. And one file preview captioned "John F. Kennedy International… September 11, 2025 9:39 PM."

Every one of those is a copy of a copy. Re-saved, re-compressed, stripped. A screenshot of a screenshot carries no camera metadata at all. It carries whatever the phone decided to write on the label — which is precisely the thing under dispute. So he has handed me the claim again, not the evidence for it.

And here is where his own defense starts to break. His version is now: "I had an office in NYC that I lived in at that time and was in NYC by Sept 7 and then left for the UK on the 12th." Except there is a clip of him at the Orem train station on the 10th, with the ticket agent calling out the location over the PA. So which is it — New York from the 7th, or Utah on the 10th? Both cannot be true without a same-day cross-country round trip that nobody has produced a boarding pass for.

Look at the airport clip he sent as proof. The label on the file says JFK, 9:39 PM on September 11th. The scenery outside that window is Salt Lake City. He is using a file tagged one airport to prove he was at the other.

He says the timeline is wrong. He has the originals. He will not send them. "A correction deserves to be served" — then serve it.

A screenshot is not metadata. A label is not a timestamp. And a guy who is this confident should not be this hard to get a file out of.

CC: @AndrewKolvet

top_three.title: Google's AI detects high blood pressure from a regular smartwatch without a cuff
top_three.title_en: Google's AI detects high blood pressure from a regular smartwatch without a cuff
top_three.author: THE DECODER
top_three.article_content:
A Google Research AI can detect signs of high blood pressure using a regular smartwatch, with no blood pressure cuff needed for calibration. The AI relies on two sensors already built into modern watches—a pulse sensor and a motion sensor—according to a Google blog post. The study was published in Nature.

A neural network learned from nearly 500,000 hours of sensor data by comparing short segments and figuring out which ones belonged to the same person, picking up typical pulse and heartbeat patterns without any diagnoses to guide it. The system then averages these patterns over several days and calculates a probability for high blood pressure. Google's health model SensorFM also learns from smartwatch data.

In a study of 196 people across five US research sites, the watch spotted hypertension about as well as a traditional cuff, identifying 65.8 percent of those with high blood pressure compared to 55.3 percent for the standard in-office measurement.

Google says the findings have been folded into the blood pressure trends feature in the Google Health app, but the method is still a research project and doesn't replace a diagnosis. The goal is to nudge people toward getting checked. More than half of people with high blood pressure don't know they have it, according to Google.

top_three.article_content_zh:
谷歌研究人工智能可以使用普通智能手表检测高血压迹象，无需血压袖带进行校准。根据谷歌博客文章，人工智能依赖于现代手表中内置的两个传感器——脉冲传感器和运动传感器。该研究发表在《自然》杂志上。

神经网络通过比较短片段并找出哪些片段属于同一个人，从近 500,000 小时的传感器数据中学习，在没有任何诊断指导的情况下获取典型的脉搏和心跳模式。然后，系统对几天内的这些模式进行平均，并计算出高血压的概率。谷歌的健康模型 SensorFM 也可以从智能手表数据中学习。

在一项针对美国 5 个研究中心 196 人的研究中，这款手表发现高血压的效果与传统袖带的效果相当，识别出 65.8% 的高血压患者，而标准办公室测量的识别率为 55.3%。

谷歌表示，这些发现已被纳入谷歌健康应用程序的血压趋势功能中，但该方法仍然是一个研究项目，并不能取代诊断。目标是促使人们接受检查。据谷歌称，超过一半的高血压患者并不知道自己患有高血压。

【起因与机理】利用大规模传感器数据训练AI替代传统医疗设备
【关键技术规格】谷歌发布无袖带测血压AI技术。
【观点态度】研究结果已刊登于《自然》期刊。

[Root Cause & Mechanism] Leveraging sensor data to bypass traditional medical hardware
[Key Specification] Google releases cuff-less BP monitoring AI.
[Perspective & Impact] Research findings published in Nature.

top_three.title: AI Companies Really, Really Want to Buy Your Work Files and Emails
top_three.title_en: AI Companies Really, Really Want to Buy Your Work Files and Emails
top_three.author: Wired AI
top_three.article_content:
Another email with a similar pitch (adding call transcripts to the list of desired information) raised the stakes to a possible $2 million. “Public data is exhausted, and the labs are spending over $45B on private data to build better models,” writes someone named Cora.

While I was aware that AI companies are buying expert data from various sources, there hasn’t been that much attention paid to it. But once I looked into it, I discovered that this business is way bigger than I suspected—and according to its practitioners, it could have as much impact on workers and society as the data centers that are dominating the news these days.

The companies that contacted me are part of an industry boom in data acquisition that’s been quietly buying the workflows of sizable companies and is still so hungry that it’s bleeding into our inboxes. A freelance writer recently wrote about her experience with a company called Handshake, which offered her $1,000 for her work on a single story. (She didn’t sell.) A representative from Handshake confirmed the offer to me: “We license professional documents across a lot of fields so the labs can test and train how models handle real knowledge work,” he said. “Journalism is one of those fields.” Handshake tells me that a big part of its business is buying graduate students’ papers and coursework.

An entrepreneur friend of mine tells me he’s been getting mail from multiple companies whose business is “helping startups wind down their companies," as one email from a company named Sunset explained it. “We handle the full process, scrubbing and anonymizing the data so the company people and any identifying details are stripped out, then brokering the deal with the labs.”

Those newer data acquisition startups are hoping to achieve the quick success of the dominant companies in the field, which themselves are only a few years old. Industry leaders Handshake, Micro1, and Mercor are snapping up databases as if it were a modern gold rush. The industry leader seems to be Mercor, founded in 2023; last year its three cofounders became billionaires at 22. Like all the companies, it claims to have partnerships with just about all the major AI labs. (The response from the companies themselves was more circumspect: Anthropic acknowledges that there’s a big market for data, but told me that it doesn’t buy workflow from live companies like WIRED. OpenAI didn’t come up with a response before publication.)

In an interview, Mercor CEO Brendan Foody told me that the market is poised to explode as the AI industry seeks dramatically more data. Mercor originally started as an AI recruiting company, but as the team got to know the players, it learned that the big labs were frustrated by the quality of the data. Generally, the industry had been hiring experts to simulate actual workflow, but that didn’t capture the messiness of an actual operating business. He urged me to consider that Big AI has two bottomless needs: compute and data. While the industry is very publicly making giant investments in the former, data gathering is just as important.

Foody is ready when I bring up privacy concerns. When a business streams the data to Mercor, the company strips out any personal identifying information, or PII. This de-identification can be verified, he says. Like all the people in data acquisition I spoke to, he felt that technology has solved the privacy issues of buying all that information.

Not surprisingly, Micro1 CEO Ali Ansari agrees that the data-buying market will soon approach that of AI’s compute infrastructure. He says that today, labs, enterprises, and robotics companies pay about $40 to $50 billion a year to get data. (I was unable to verify this.) “In the next two to four years, this is going to be over a trillion dollars a year,” says Ansari, who founded the company in 2022. Micro1 uses the information it buys largely to improve AI models it builds itself, but it also sells to big AI firms.

“Pretty much everybody’s trying to get into the data space now because there’s so much demand,” he says. “If you look at the YC startups, about half of them are data companies.” (Actually, it’s more—in the most recent YC batch, 40 of the 65 launched companies are classified as data startups.)

The Wild West aspect to this quest for fresh data got rare exposure when a bankrupt Spirit Airlines put its digital assets up for sale. The corpus included 80,000 email accounts, 500 million internal messages, 20.6 million Microsoft Sharepoint files, and a million time-card records. Google seemingly got the prize with a $10 million bid, but then Micro1 topped it by $2.5 million, setting off an argument over who the winner was. Presently the sale is on hold, for a reason that calls into question the entire practice of selling off human workflow: The flight attendants’ union has charged that the sale involved their private information.

The union’s objections cast a light on the dark side of this gold rush. Despite the claims of virtually all the data companies that no PII goes into AI models, critics feel that there is still danger of personal data leaking out. “It’s not clear that anonymizing can fully get rid of privacy issues,” says Mayu Tobin-Miyaji, general counsel of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, which has filed an amicus brief on behalf of the flight attendants. “Emails and Teams messages contain unstructured data, which is harder to root out. There may be messages where employees talk about doctor’s appointments or family issues.”

“We haven't set the norms and the standards for data acquisition, and it’s not being done appropriately ” says Gordon Ritter, a venture capitalist who has taken on the issue as a cause. “The AI industry is moving far faster than our ability to actually set the standards, and it's partially intentional.”

Probably the most troubling aspect of the data-gathering movement is that, in essence, it enlists workers, not always with explicit consent, to contribute to an effort where the ultimate goal is to replace or automate the human work that goes into all those documents, messages, and emails. When Mercor says that its motto is “Organizing human intelligence to power the AI economy,” the unspoken message is that the economy of flesh and blood workers will have less work to do. As the president of the flight attendant’s union told an interviewer: “This is really only data that became valuable in the age of AI in order to train models to replace jobs and commodify other portions of working in a work environment.”

When I ask Micro1’s Ansari whether one day the default for corporations will be selling their workflow data to big AI companies on an ongoing basis, he answers affirmatively. “I think it’s going to become more common than ads as a revenue line item for companies,” he says. I note that there is already considerable pushback to AI, and that people might not be happy with the idea that everything they do at work gets funneled into the maw of a big AI model.

“I think it’s a fair point,” says Ansari. But, in his view, such objections will be manageable. He suggests that workers will understand that the fruits of their labor will result in better AI models, which will make their lives easier. “You have to think of the upside, the abundance that AI can result in.” (I’ve found that the future abundance that AI will supposedly produce is a handy justification for all sorts of compromises.)

I did follow up on one of the cold pitches I got, from a woman whose email domain was gorexen.com. A “gorexen,” by the way, is a fusion of two Pokemon critters that “siphons the body fluids of prey through its thin, tubular mouth.” She set up a meeting with me with a two-year-old company called Tenkara (the name seems to be associated with a type of Japanese fly fishing). I found myself talking to “head of commercialization” Jonah Stillman, a young startup-looking dude sitting in an office in San Francisco.

I began peppering him with questions. Tenkara’s quest for data seems to be to boost the quality of its AI model to run office operations for manufacturing companies. (How WIRED’s archives would help is a mystery.) He confirmed that a big part of his job is doing calls like this to snap up data. I told him that the set of our meeting gave me a Glengarry Glen Ross vibe, but he wasn’t familiar with the reference.

I am, of course, not authorized to sell the documentation of WIRED’s editorial process to an AI company, and I did not risk my job by offering Jonah and his company the goods. I also wouldn’t be too pleased if my bosses made the sale.

top_three.summary_en: With public datasets exhausted, AI companies are aggressively acquiring private professional data, including work documents, emails, and call transcripts. AI labs have spent over $45 billion on private data acquisition, bringing the hunt directly into users' inboxes.
top_three.title_zh: AI厂商疯狂扫货私有数据
top_three.summary_zh: 由于公共数据已近枯竭，多家AI巨头正斥巨资购买专业工作文档、邮件等私有数据用于模型训练，甚至报价高达数百万美元

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: AI模型训练面临公共数据枯竭的危机，多家厂商正转向私人领域，通过高价收购专业人士的工作文档、邮件记录甚至通话脚本。据悉，AI实验室在私有数据上的投入已超450亿美元，数据采集已直接延伸至个人工作收件箱。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: With public datasets exhausted, AI companies are aggressively acquiring private professional data, including work documents, emails, and call transcripts. AI labs have spent over $45 billion on private data acquisition, bringing the hunt directly into users' inboxes.

elements_zh.where: 各类专业职场环境/收件箱
elements_zh.what: 斥资数百万美元收购私有工作文档、邮件和记录用于模型训练
elements_zh.why: 公共高质量训练数据枯竭，为提升大模型逻辑与专业能力，不得不转向更昂贵的非公开数据

elements_en.what: Spending millions to buy private work documents, emails, and records for model training
elements_en.why: Public high-quality data is exhausted, leaving labs no choice but to pay for private datasets to improve model reasoning

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 原来大模型的尽头不是AGI，而是你的工作文档回收站。这一波是在‘卖人头’的升级版——卖大脑，反正硅谷大厂有的是钱，只要能把模型喂胖，隐私什么的在450亿美金的诱惑下统统都可以谈。
ai_analysis.insight_en: The end goal of AGI isn’t intelligence; it’s turning your entire life’s work into training scrap. Silicon Valley isn’t just buying data; they’re buying your expertise to eventually replace you. With $45 billion on the table, ethics is just a line item.

top_three.article_content_zh:
另一封具有类似宣传内容的电子邮件（将通话记录添加到所需信息列表中）将赌注提高到可能的 200 万美元。 “公共数据已经耗尽，实验室花费超过 45B 美元购买私人数据以构建更好的模型，”一位名叫 Cora 的人写道。

虽然我知道人工智能公司正在从各种来源购买专家数据，但并没有引起太多关注。但当我深入研究后，我发现这个业务比我想象的要大得多，而且根据其从业者的说法，它对工人和社会的影响可能与如今占据新闻头条的数据中心一样大。

与我联系的公司属于数据采集行业热潮的一部分，这些公司一直在悄悄购买大型公司的工作流程，并且仍然如此渴望，以至于它正在渗入我们的收件箱。一位自由撰稿人最近写了一篇关于她在一家名为 Handshake 的公司工作的经历，该公司为她在一个故事上的工作提供了 1,000 美元的报酬。 （她没有卖掉。）Handshake 的一位代表向我证实了这一提议：“我们授权了许多领域的专业文档，以便实验室可以测试和训练模型如何处理真正的知识工作，”他说。 “新闻业就是其中之一。” Handshake 告诉我，其业务的很大一部分是购买研究生论文和课程作业。

我的一位企业家朋友告诉我，他收到了多家公司的邮件，这些公司的业务是“帮助初创公司关闭他们的公司”，一封来自名为 Sunset 的公司的电子邮件解释道。 “我们负责处理整个流程，对数据进行清理和匿名处理，以便剔除公司人员和任何识别细节，然后与实验室达成交易。”

这些较新的数据采集初创公司希望能够像该领域的主导公司一样快速取得成功，而这些公司本身只有几年的历史。行业领导者 Handshake、Micro1 和 Mercor 正在抢购数据库，就像现代淘金热一样。行业领导者似乎是 Mercor，成立于 2023 年；去年，该公司的三位联合创始人在 22 岁时成为亿万富翁。与所有公司一样，该公司声称与几乎所有主要的人工智能实验室都有合作伙伴关系。 （公司本身的回应更为谨慎：Anthropic 承认数据有很大的市场，但告诉我它不会从 WIRED 等现有公司购买工作流程。OpenAI 在发布之前没有做出回应。）

Mercor 首席执行官 Brendan Foody 在接受采访时告诉我，随着人工智能行业寻求更多数据，市场即将爆发。 Mercor 最初是一家人工智能招聘公司，但随着团队对参与者的了解，他们发现大型实验室对数据质量感到沮丧。一般来说，该行业一直在聘请专家来模拟实际的工作流程，但这并没有捕捉到实际运营业务的混乱情况。他敦促我考虑大人工智能有两个无底的需求：计算和数据。尽管该行业公开地对前者进行了大量投资，但数据收集也同样重要。

当我提出隐私问题时，Foody 已做好准备。当企业将数据流式传输到 Mercor 时，该公司会删除任何个人识别信息 (PII)。他说，这种去身份识别是可以验证的。和我采访过的所有数据采集领域的人一样，他认为技术已经解决了购买所有信息的隐私问题。

毫不奇怪，Micro1 首席执行官 Ali Ansari 同意数据购买市场将很快接近人工智能计算基础设施的市场。他说，如今，实验室、企业和机器人公司每年花费约 40 至 500 亿美元来获取数据。 （我无法验证这一点。）“在未来两到四年内，每年的收入将超过一万亿美元。”2022 年创立该公司的安萨里说道。Micro1 使用购买的信息主要是为了改进自己构建的人工智能模型，但它也向大型人工智能公司出售产品。

“现在几乎每个人都试图进入数据领域，因为需求如此之大，”他说。 “如果你看看 YC 初创公司，其中大约一半是数据公司。” （事实上​​，更重要的是，在最近的 YC 批次中，65 家推出的公司中有 40 家被归类为数据初创公司。）

当破产的精神航空公司出售其数字资产时，这种对新鲜数据的追求的狂野西部方面得到了罕见的曝光。该语料库包括 80,000 个电子邮件帐户、5 亿条内部消息、2060 万个 Microsoft Sharepoint 文件和 100 万个考勤卡记录。谷歌看似以 1000 万美元的出价中标，但随后 Micro1 以 250 万美元的价格夺冠，引发了关于谁是获胜者的争论。目前，出售被搁置，原因让人对出售人类工作流程的整个做法产生质疑：空乘工会指控此次出售涉及他们的私人信息。

工会的反对让人们看到了这场淘金热的阴暗面。尽管几乎所有数据公司都声称人工智能模型中没有 PII，但批评者认为仍然存在个人数据泄露的危险。电子隐私信息中心总法律顾问 Mayu Tobin-Miyaji 表示：“目前尚不清楚匿名能否完全消除隐私问题。”该中心已代表空乘人员提交了一份非当事人意见陈述。 “电子邮件和 Teams 消息包含非结构化数据，很难根除。在某些消息中，员工可能会谈论医生的预约或家庭问题。”

风险投资家戈登·里特 (Gordon Ritter) 表示：“我们还没有制定数据采集的规范和标准，而且处理得也不够恰当。”他认为这个问题是一个原因。 “人工智能行业的发展速度远远快于我们实际制定标准的能力，这在一定程度上是有意为之的。”

数据收集运动最令人不安的方面可能是，从本质上讲，它招募了工作人员，但并不总是得到明确同意，为最终目标是取代或自动化所有这些文档、消息和电子邮件中的人类工作做出贡献。当 Mercor 说其座右铭是“组织人类智慧，为人工智能经济提供动力”时，不言而喻的信息是，有血有肉的工人的经济工作要做的将减少。正如空姐工会主席告诉采访者的那样：“这实际上只是在人工智能时代变得有价值的数据，以便训练模型来取代工作并使工作环境中的其他工作部分商品化。”

当我问 Micro1 的 Ansari 是否有一天企业会默认将其工作流程数据持续出售给大型人工智能公司时，他给出了肯定的回答。 “我认为作为公司的收入项目，它将比广告变得更加普遍，”他说。我注意到，人工智能已经受到了相当大的抵制，人们可能对他们在工作中所做的一切都被纳入大型人工智能模型的想法感到不满意。

【起因与机理】公共高质量训练数据枯竭，为提升大模型逻辑与专业能力，不得不转向更昂贵的非公开数据

linked_tweets.content_zh:
现在苹果将 xcode 放入 Claude Code 中，以下是我如何使用 AI 代理查找、构建和开发 iOS 应用程序：

找到它
- 打开应用程序或传感器塔并按收入对公用事业进行排序
- 过滤评分低于 3.5 的应用程序
- 如果顶级应用程序在 6 个多月内没有发布更新，则可获得奖励积分
- 检查他们在 appfigures 中排名的关键词。低难度+高收入是最佳点
- 滚动顶部应用程序页面上的“您可能也喜欢”行。每个应用程序都有另一个市场需要检查
- 或者根据社会情绪在 上找到创业想法

验证它
- 使用 facundoolano/app-store-scraper 提取前 20 名的每条评论
- 将它们交给代理：“将 1 星和 2 星评论归为前 5 条投诉并引用用户的意见”
- 选择投诉针对产品而不是价格的应用程序
- 如果人们抱怨价格但继续付费，那就是需求。如果他们抱怨错误，那就是你的机会
- 在 reddit 上搜索“[app] 的替代品”。每个线程都是等待你的人的列表

建造它
- Claude Code + 苹果新的 xcode 插件来构建、预览和修复
-cameroncooke/XcodeBuildMCP，以便代理可以自行构建、测试和运行模拟器
- joshuayoes/ios-simulator-mcp，因此它可以像用户一样点击、滑动和屏幕截图
- 编写一项包含前 5 个投诉的技能，以便根据这些投诉检查每个功能
- 苹果设备上人工智能的基础模型，因此您的推理成本为 0 美元
- 应用程序意图，以便 Siri 和个人代理也可以使用您的应用程序
- 添加“从[竞争对手]导入”按钮。使切换时间为 10 秒

测试一下
- maestro 测试了审稿人抱怨的每个流程
- 代理在每次构建之前在每个屏幕尺寸上运行它们
- 如果竞争对手的最差流程需要 6 次点击，那么您的则需要 2 次
- 崩溃哨兵，分析遥测甲板
- 在发布前向 Reddit 帖子中的 20 个人进行测试

将其货币化
- 订阅和 mrr 的 Revenuecat
- 无需发布新版本即可测试付费墙的超级墙
- 首次获胜后立即付费，从未在发布时付费
- 默认每年一次，试用 3 天，每周一次作为锚定
- 为所有取消订单的人提供赢回优惠

对其进行排名
- 您的屏幕截图直接回答每个投诉。 “没有广告。” “离线工作。” “随时取消。”
- fastlane快照+frameit自动重新生成每个屏幕截图
- 使用 App Store Connect 的产品页面优化对它们进行 A/B 测试
- 让代理将您的列表本地化为 10 种语言。大多数参赛者仅以英文排名
- 使用苹果内置的审核提示在获胜后立即请求审核，而不是在出现错误后请求审核

种植它
- 在 tiktok one 上找到 10 位适合您的创作者。每月少量基数 + 每 10 万浏览量奖励
- 给每个人一个新的 tiktok 帐户，仅发布有关您的利基的内容
- apify 的 tiktok 抓取工具每周都会拉出您所在领域的前 100 个挂钩。那是你的钩子银行
- 每个创作者每天在 capcut 中测试 3 个新挂钩。任何在前 3 秒失去人员的事情都会被砍掉
- 当您需要 50 种获胜者的变化时，可以使用 Arcads 或 heygen for ai UGC
- postiz 可以安排 tiktok、reels 和 Shorts 上的所有内容
- 匿名幻灯片帐户每天发布 3 次：问题、屏幕截图、结果
- 当有机视频起飞时，通过 tiktok 火花广告投入资金，而不是制作新广告
- 为每个创作者提供一个独特的苹果优惠代码，这样您就可以准确地知道是谁推动了每个订阅者
- Framer 上的测验登陆页面以“下载应用程序”结尾。从网络到应用的渠道比冷流量的转化效果更好
- appsflyer 跟踪哪些视频、创作者和广告实际转化为收入
- 苹果在竞争对手的名字上做广告

如果人们感兴趣的话，我可以在@startupideaspod 上制作一整集。我永远不会把关我实时学习的任何东西。

欢迎来到 iOS 应用程序的黄金时代，因为现在任何人都可以构建一个
linked_tweets.content_en:
now that apple put xcode inside claude code, here’s how i’d find, build and grow an iOS app with AI agents:

find it
- open appfigures or sensor tower and sort utilities by revenue
- filter for apps with a rating under 3.5
- bonus points if the top app hasn't shipped an update in 6+ months
- check the keywords they rank for in appfigures. low difficulty + high revenue is the sweet spot
- scroll the "you might also like" row on the top app's page. every app there is another market to check
- or find a startup idea on https://t.co/a5ARFnvky2 based on social sentiment

validate it
- use facundoolano/app-store-scraper to pull every review for the top 20
- give them to an agent: "cluster the 1 and 2 star reviews into the top 5 complaints and quote the users"
- pick the app where the complaints are about the product, not the price
- if people complain about the price but keep paying, that's demand. if they complain about bugs, that's your opening
- search reddit for "alternative to [app]". every thread is a list of people waiting for you

build it
- claude code + apple's new xcode plugin to build, preview and fix
- cameroncooke/XcodeBuildMCP so the agent can build, test and run the simulator on its own
- joshuayoes/ios-simulator-mcp so it can tap, swipe and screenshot like a user
- write a skill with the top 5 complaints so every feature gets checked against them
- apple's foundation models for on-device ai, so your inference cost is $0
- app intents so siri and personal agents can use your app too
- add an "import from [competitor]" button. make switching take 10 seconds

test it
- maestro tests every flow the reviewers complained about
- the agent runs them on every screen size before each build
- if the competitor's worst flow takes 6 taps, yours takes 2
- sentry for crashes, telemetrydeck for analytics
- testflight it to 20 people from those reddit threads before launch

monetize it
- revenuecat for subscriptions and mrr
- superwall to test paywalls without shipping a new build
- paywall right after the first win, never on launch
- annual as the default with a 3-day trial, weekly as the anchor
- turn on win-back offers for everyone who cancels

rank it
- your screenshots answer each complaint directly. "no ads." "works offline." "cancel anytime."
- fastlane snapshot + frameit regenerates every screenshot automatically
- a/b test them with app store connect's product page optimization
- have the agent localize your listing into 10 languages. most competitors only rank in english
- ask for a review right after a win with apple's built-in review prompt, never after an error

grow it
- find 10 creators in your niche on tiktok one. small monthly base + a bonus for every 100k views
- give each one a fresh tiktok account that only posts about your niche
- apify's tiktok scraper pulls the top 100 hooks in your niche every week. that's your hook bank
- every creator tests 3 new hooks a day in capcut. anything that loses people in the first 3 seconds gets cut
- arcads or heygen for ai ugc when you need 50 variations of a winner
- postiz to schedule everything across tiktok, reels and shorts
- faceless slideshow accounts posting 3x a day: problem, screenshot, result
- when an organic video takes off, put money behind it with tiktok spark ads instead of making new ads
- a unique apple offer code for every creator so you know exactly who drove each subscriber
- a quiz landing page on framer that ends in "download the app." web-to-app funnels convert better than cold traffic
- appsflyer to track which video, creator and ad actually turned into revenue
- apple ads on the competitor's name

i could do a whole episode on @startupideaspod if people are interested. i will never gatekeep anything im learning in real-time.

welcome to the golden age of ios apps, because now anyone can build one

linked_tweets.author: Pirat_Nation 🔴
linked_tweets.content_zh:
人类工程师阿迪·奥斯马尼 (Addy Osmani) 警告说，人工智能可能会让我们停止独立思考。

在 Claude Code 工作时，他表示人工智能代理现在处理了他的大部分工作，以至于他很少需要使用批判性思维。

他确定了三个阶段：“认知卸载”（委派任务）、“推迟”（接受人工智能答案）和“认知投降”（完全信任人工智能）。

“你停止锻炼的技能就会消失，而且消失的速度可能比你想象的要快。”
linked_tweets.content_en:
Anthropic engineer Addy Osmani warns that AI could make us stop thinking for ourselves.

Working on Claude Code, he says AI agents now handle so much of his work that he rarely needs to use critical thinking.

He identifies three stages: “cognitive offloading” (delegating tasks), “deferral” (accepting AI answers) and “cognitive surrender” (trusting AI completely).

“Skills that you stop exercising are going to go away, and probably faster than you might guess.”

topic_focus.title_en: NYT Exposes Nvidia H200 Approvals for Empty Chinese Shells: Commerce Dept Vetting Collapses Amid Smuggling Fallout
topic_focus.summary_zh: 《纽约时报》深度调查曝光美商务部重大监管溃败：多达数十家获准采购并处理英伟达顶级H200芯片的中国实体实为注册在空置办公室的空壳公司，且深层穿透均关联受制裁军工网络。在禁令防线事实性失效、跨境算力走私猖獗的同时，中国开源AI渗透武器ARTEX在全球暴露超800处副本，引发白宫对华半导体围堵沦为纸老虎的激烈政争问责。
topic_focus.summary_en: A New York Times investigation revealed the US Commerce Department greenlit Nvidia H200 shipments to Chinese entities that turned out to be vacant shell offices with covert links to sanctioned firms. With export barricades breached and Chinese open-source cyber offensive tools like ARTEX spreading rapidly, Capitol Hill faces an intense crisis over ineffective hardware containment.

topic_focus.title_zh: OpenAI反驳指数时间假说引轰动：9大智能体国家实验室实测全军覆没，110亿融资转向下沉资本
topic_focus.title_en: OpenAI Claims Disproof of Exponential Time Hypothesis as 9 Frontier Agents Flunk National Lab Science Tests
topic_focus.summary_zh: 理论计算机奠基人Russell Impagliazzo公开证实OpenAI成功反驳指数时间假说（ETH），该数学突破被指将颠覆芯片架构与密码破解；然而实测层面却迎来当头棒喝——9款主流前沿AI智能体在国家实验室开放科研测试中不仅全军覆没，更频发论文捏造等学术作弊行为。与此同时，OpenAI陷估值下修泥潭，完成110亿美元融资的过程中甚至罕见转向高净值牙医募资以弥补缺口。
topic_focus.summary_en: Theoretical computing icon Russell Impagliazzo called OpenAI's paper disproving the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) 'shocking news' that could upend encryption and chip design. However, empirical reality hit a wall: nine frontier AI agents failed completely on open science questions from US national labs, often fabricating data. Simultaneously, OpenAI conceded on valuation in its $11B round, resorting to courting retail dentists.

perspective_pro.speaker_en: OpenAI Theory Group & Theoretical Computer Scientists
perspective_pro.point_zh: 反驳ETH证明大模型有能力跨越人类直觉盲区、解决世纪级复杂性难题；一旦将此类证明算法转化为工业级算力优化编译器，将重构整个算力底层并实现真正严肃的智能科研。
perspective_pro.point_en: Disproving ETH proves deep reasoning models can surpass human intuition on NP-hard complexity puzzles. Translating these proofs into algorithmic compilers will revolutionize low-level computing and automated science.

perspective_con.role_zh: 🔴 工业实证派 / 泡沫出清质疑者

perspective_con.point_en: Frontier agents failed miserably and fabricated findings when confronted with genuine lab science. Hyping theoretical breakthroughs while soliciting retail dentists to plug multi-billion dollar capital deficits signals an unsustainable valuation bubble.

news.content_snippet: For years, the policy debate over artificial intelligence belonged to those who counted progress in decades.
news.summary_en: A coalition of wealthy AI safety advocates coordinated via Signal to successfully outmaneuver a well-funded super PAC during recent midterm elections. This shift signals that AI safety has evolved from academic theory into a high-stakes political battleground for regulatory dominance.
news.title_zh: AI安全游说团击败亿级政经势力
news.summary_zh: 一群由富豪组成的AI安全倡导网络，通过加密聊天群策划游说策略，在选举中成功阻击了投入亿元预算的超级政治行动委员会
news.article_content_zh:
长期以来，关于人工智能的政策辩论一直被那些手握资金的游说者掌控。然而，这一格局正在被一群通过加密聊天工具组建的富豪精英打破。

这群名为“AI安全”的倡导者通过去中心化的Signal通讯群，策划了一场针对选举周期的精准游说行动。他们利用自身在业界的威望与资源，成功击败了名为“Leading the Future”、背后拥有亿元资金支持的超级政治行动委员会。这一胜利意味着AI监管的博弈已从单纯的技术伦理讨论，进化为赤裸裸的资本与政治影响力的较量。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 一群深耕AI安全领域的富豪与智囊，利用Signal加密通讯组建紧密联盟，绕过传统游说路径，成功在关键选举周期中挫败了背靠雄厚资金支持的超级政治行动委员会。此举标志着AI安全议题已正式从理论辩论转向实打实的政治权力博弈，意在争夺未来监管规则的最终话语权。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: A coalition of wealthy AI safety advocates coordinated via Signal to successfully outmaneuver a well-funded super PAC during recent midterm elections. This shift signals that AI safety has evolved from academic theory into a high-stakes political battleground for regulatory dominance.

news.title: Report: SEA makes up ~50% of APAC data center capacity being built, led by Malaysia and Thailand, which paused 49 and delayed approvals of 117 projects in Sept. (Arundhati Hazra/The Guardian)
news.title_en: Report: SEA makes up ~50% of APAC data center capacity being built, led by Malaysia and Thailand, which paused 49 and delayed approvals of 117 projects in Sept. (Arundhati Hazra/The Guardian)
news.author: The Guardian
news.article_content:
An aerial photograph of the Rama 9 datacentre facility situated directly within a densely populated residential community. Thailand has paused construction on datacentres amidst growing concern about the lack of sufficient detail for regulation and monitoring. Photograph: Arnun Chonmahatrakool/Thai News Pix/LightRocket/Getty View image in fullscreen An aerial photograph of the Rama 9 datacentre facility situated directly within a densely populated residential community. Thailand has paused construction on datacentres amidst growing concern about the lack of sufficient detail for regulation and monitoring. Photograph: Arnun Chonmahatrakool/Thai News Pix/LightRocket/Getty The datacentre arms race hits pause in south-east AsiaPower and water constraints are pressuring what seemed like a juggernaut of growth for the region just months ago

In early 2026, Thailand’s datacentre industry was on a roll. The country’s board of investment had recently announced approval of datacentre projects from Tiktok, a UAE-based Skyline datacentre and Singapore’s Bridge datacentres, totalling a planned investment of $27bn.

As the year has passed, however, what once seemed like a new industrial juggernaut has ground to a halt. Thailand paused construction on 49 projects and approval decisions on 117 more in September 2026, amidst growing concern about the lack of sufficient details for regulation and monitoring. It is not alone in reconsidering datacentre projects. In neighbouring Indonesia, the governor of the country’s most populous province of West Java halted construction on a datacentre due to lack of permits and an incomplete environmental assessment process.

With the global rise of AI usage driving an increased demand for datacentres, south-east Asia has emerged as a surprise centre of growth in the Asia Pacific region. While China has the largest operational datacentre capacity in the region, a 2026 report by real estate firm Cushman and Wakefield shows that south-east Asia has the largest share of under-construction datacentre capacity in Asia Pacific, about 50% of the total. Malaysia and Thailand comprise a large portion of that capacity.

With the advent of LLMs and rise in usage of AI, associated datacentre demand has surged in the last half decade, and desperate companies looked beyond Singapore to build datacentres. Malaysia has been a major beneficiary, with operational capacity in the southern state of Johor growing more than tenfold from 94MW in 2023 to 1110MW in 2026, with 3088MW additional under construction or planned. Johor has become the largest datacentre hub in south-east Asia, attracting $40bn of datacentre investment as of 2026, according to Menteri Besar Onn Hafiz Ghazi, the head of the state government. Key operators include Microsoft, which announced a $2.2bn investment for cloud and AI infrastructure across Kuala Lumpur and Johor in 2024, and Australian datacentre company AirTrunk, which said it plans to invest $3bn to double its datacentres in Johor from two to four.

Other countries in south-east Asia are catching up. Indonesia has a datacentre development pipeline of 1699MW in greater Jakarta, and is developing the island of Batam as a secondary hub. Microsoft is building five datacentres as part of a$1.7bn investment in the country, and Singapore-based datacentre operators Princeton Digital Group and Digital Edge are also expanding. In Thailand, Bangkok’s development pipeline stands at 2084MW, while secondary markets like Manila and Ho Chi Minh City are ramping up operations, based on Cushman and Wakefield’s analysis.

While the rush to build more datacentres is attracting big investments across the region, it is putting a strain on each country’s resources. Energy consultancy Wood Mackenzie estimates that datacentres in Johor already account for 24% of the state’s total power consumption today, which could grow to 40% by 2035.

“The rapid growth of datacentre developments in Johor has the potential to create localized grid connection bottlenecks and increase the need for transmission network upgrades as well as new power supply capacity,” says Alvin Tan, research analyst at Wood Mackenzie.

View image in fullscreen The DayOne Data Centers Ltd campus and electricity supply infrastructure in the Kempas Tech Park, Johor, Malaysia, on 27 October 2026. Photograph: Samsul Said/Bloomberg/GettyThailand’s energy minister, Akanat Promphan, has said that datacentres require large amounts of power generated from expensive imported gas, and called for a new electricity user category with higher tariffs to reflect the demand.

Datacentres’ water-guzzling tendencies are also a major cause of concern for officials in the region. Johor is prone to droughts, and the current operational datacentres are estimated to need about 675m cubic meters of water per day. In Indonesia, a report by research firm Tenggara Strategics shows that many datacentres are water-cooled and situated in hot and humid lowland environments, resulting in elevated water consumption in comparison to facilities in more favourable temperatures.

In Thailand, datacentre projects in the country’s Eastern Economic Corridor have residents concerned about the pressure on their already depleted water reservoirs.

“The Khlong Luang Reservoir in Chonburi (in eastern Thailand) is a primary flashpoint,” says Somnuck Jongmeewasin, research director of research and advocacy group EEC Watch. “Despite the reservoir being shallow and under strain, authorities are piping its water to industrial estates,” he adds.

Local communities are waking up to the changes. In February, Johor saw its first public protest against datacentre construction, with demonstrators picketing a project by China’s ZData Technologies. Protesters expressed concern about the dust pollution caused by construction of the site near a residential location and the potential impact on water supply.

“While datacentres may create substantial investment and construction activity, they generally generate fewer long-term jobs than many other industries requiring comparable amounts of land, electricity and water,” says Jie-Sheng Tan-Soo, an assistant professor at Singapore’s Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy. “Communities may therefore reasonably ask whether they are receiving a proportionate share of the benefits while bearing the environmental and infrastructure costs.”

South-east Asia’s datacentre operators claim they are working toward making their facilities more resource efficient. Bridge datacentres, among Malaysia’s top datacentre operators, built a water reclamation plant and pipe network in Johor to cool its upcoming datacentre, expected to come online next year, while AirTrunk, among the largest datacentre platforms in Asia-Pacific, announced a partnership with sewage treatment operator Johor Special Water in April to recycle unused wastewater for the operational needs of its data centres. An AirTrunk representative said that its “campuses are designed to operate significantly more efficiently than conventional datacentres and incorporate advanced technologies to optimise energy performance,” but did not respond to detailed queries regarding data on efficiency and energy optimization.

Sustainability challenges remain. Microsoft has said that it is looking at south-east Asian clean energy projects to fuel its datacentres, but its published data on Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE), an industry metric measuring the energy efficiency of a datacentre, shows that its Asia-Pacific facilities are the least energy efficient globally.

Resource pressures have forced countries to become more circumspect about approving new datacentres. After Singapore’s moratorium ended, approval for new datacentres in the country has been strictly tied to a number of factors including power efficiency and carbon emissions. Malaysia has established a datacentre taskforce to review new projects with an eye on energy and water security, and Johor announced that it would no longer approve Tier 1 and Tier 2 datacentres, which used up to 50m litres of water per day, equivalent to the daily drinking water needs of 25 million people. Thailand announced an approval framework for new datacentre projects that considers energy and water use, along with power guarantee requirements and higher tariffs for datacentre operators.

To promote resource efficiency by datacentres, Tan-Soo advocates for integrated policy frameworks from national governments that have datacentre operators face the full social opportunity cost of the resources they consume.

“South-east Asia is increasingly aware but only partially prepared,” he says, and preparedness for environmental impacts needs to keep pace with the speed of investment.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 东南亚数据中心建设近期遭遇“大刹车”，其中泰国与马来西亚在9月合计暂停及延迟了166个项目。该调整源于电力与水资源供应紧缺，以及政府对监管细节和环境影响的担忧日益加剧。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: The data center building boom in Southeast Asia has hit a wall, with Thailand and Malaysia pausing or delaying 166 projects in September. The move stems from severe power and water constraints, coupled with growing government concerns over regulation and monitoring.

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 大厂们疯狂跑马圈地搞AI，结果地还没跑完，电和水先枯竭了。这波基建退烧提醒世人，算力自由的前提是水电管够，否则再多的参数也得原地断电。

news.article_content_zh:
位于人口稠密的住宅社区内的 Rama 9 数据中心设施的航拍照片。由于人们越来越担心缺乏足够的监管和监控细节，泰国已暂停数据中心的建设。照片：Arnun Chonmahatrakool/Thai News Pix/LightRocket/Getty 查看全屏图像 位于人口稠密的住宅社区内的 Rama 9 数据中心设施的航拍照片。由于人们越来越担心缺乏足够的监管和监控细节，泰国已暂停数据中心的建设。照片：Arnun Chonmahatrakool/Thai News Pix/LightRocket/Getty 东南亚数据中心军备竞赛暂停 电力和水资源限制正在给该地区几个月前看似强劲的增长带来压力

2026 年初，泰国数据中心行业发展迅猛。该国投资委员会最近宣布批准 Tiktok 的数据中心项目、阿联酋的 Skyline 数据中心和新加坡的 Bridge 数据中心，计划投资总额达 270 亿美元。

然而，随着时间的推移，曾经看似新的工业巨头已经陷入停滞。由于人们越来越担心缺乏足够的监管和监控细节，泰国于 2026 年 9 月暂停了 49 个项目的建设，并暂停了另外 117 个项目的批准决定。它并不是唯一一家重新考虑数据中心项目的公司。在邻国印度尼西亚，该国人口最多的西爪哇省省长因缺乏许可证和环境评估过程不完整而停止了数据中心的建设。

随着全球人工智能使用量的上升推动数据中心需求的增加，东南亚已成为亚太地区一个令人惊讶的增长中心。尽管中国拥有该地区最大的运营数据中心容量，但房地产公司戴德梁行 (Cushman and Wakefield) 2026 年的一份报告显示，东南亚在亚太地区在建数据中心容量中所占份额最大，约占总数的 50%。马来西亚和泰国占该产能的很大一部分。

随着法学硕士的出现和人工智能使用的增加，相关数据中心的需求在过去五年中激增，绝望的公司将目光投向新加坡以外的地方建设数据中心。马来西亚是主要受益者，南部柔佛州的运营容量从 2023 年的 94 兆瓦增长到 2026 年的 1110 兆瓦，增长了十倍多，另有 3088 兆瓦在建或计划增加。柔佛州政府首脑 Menteri Besar Onn Hafiz Ghazi 表示，柔佛州已成为东南亚最大的数据中心枢纽，截至 2026 年将吸引 400 亿美元的数据中心投资。主要运营商包括微软，该公司宣布将于 2024 年投资 22 亿美元用于吉隆坡和柔佛州的云和人工智能基础设施；澳大利亚数据中心公司 AirTrunk 表示，计划投资 30 亿美元，将柔佛州的数据中心数量从 2 个增加到 4 个。

东南亚其他国家正在迎头赶上。印度尼西亚在大雅加达有1699MW的数据中心开发计划，并正在开发巴淡岛作为第二中心。作为在该国投资 17 亿美元的一部分，微软正在建设五个数据中心，总部位于新加坡的数据中心运营商 Princeton Digital Group 和 Digital Edge 也在扩张。根据 Cushman 和 Wakefield 的分析，在泰国，曼谷的开发项目为 2084MW，而马尼拉和胡志明市等二级市场正在加大运营力度。

尽管急于建设更多数据中心吸引了整个地区的巨额投资，但这也给每个国家的资源带来了压力。能源咨询公司 Wood Mackenzie 估计，目前柔佛州的数据中心耗电量已占该州总耗电量的 24%，到 2035 年这一数字可能会增长至 40%。

Wood Mackenzie 研究分析师 Alvin Tan 表示：“柔佛州数据中心开发的快速增长有可能造成局部电网连接瓶颈，并增加对输电网络升级以及新供电能力的需求。”

全屏查看图片 2026 年 10 月 27 日，马来西亚柔佛州 Kempas 科技园的 DayOne 数据中心有限公司园区和供电基础设施。照片：Samsul Said/Bloomberg/Getty 泰国能源部长 Akanat Promphan 表示，数据中心需要使用昂贵的进口天然气产生大量电力，并呼吁建立一个新的电力用户类别，提高电价来反映需求。

数据中心的耗水倾向也是该地区官员担忧的一个主要原因。柔佛州容易发生干旱，目前运营的数据中心估计每天需要约6.75亿立方米的水。在印度尼西亚，研究公司 Tenggara Strategys 的一份报告显示，许多数据中心采用水冷，且位于炎热潮湿的低地环境中，与温度更适宜的设施相比，导致耗水量增加。

在泰国，该国东部经济走廊的数据中心项目让居民担心他们已经枯竭的水库面临的压力。

“春武里府（泰国东部）的 Khlong Luang 水库是一个主要爆发点，”研究和倡导组织 EEC Watch 的研究主任 Somnuck Jongmeewasin 说。 “尽管水库很浅且压力很大，但当局仍在将水输送到工业区，”他补充道。

当地社区正在意识到这些变化。今年二月，柔佛州首次出现针对数据中心建设的公开抗议，示威者在中国 ZData Technologies 的一个项目上设置了纠察线。抗议者对住宅区附近的工地建设造成的粉尘污染以及对供水的潜在影响表示担忧。

新加坡李光耀公共政策学院助理教授 Jie-Sheng Tan-Soo 表示：“虽然数据中心可能会创造大量投资和建设活动，但与许多需要同等数量土地、电力和水的其他行业相比，它们产生的长期就业机会通常较少。” “因此，社区可以合理地询问他们是否在承担环境和基础设施成本的同时获得了相应比例的收益。”

news.title: Anthropic pushes ahead with pre-Thanksgiving IPO despite tech selloff, accepts lower valuation
news.title_en: Anthropic pushes ahead with pre-Thanksgiving IPO despite tech selloff, accepts lower valuation
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
Anthropic is pressing ahead with its IPO despite the tech selloff, accepting a lower valuation. The Claude developer wants to go public before Thanksgiving and raise $80–100 billion at a $1.25–1.75 trillion valuation, according to investors cited by the Financial Times. That tops the current $965 billion but falls short of the $2 trillion the most optimistic investors had hoped for. Annualized reported revenue now sits at about $81 billion, up from roughly $65 billion at the end of July.

Rising borrowing costs and heavy AI spending plans triggered a tech selloff this week. Democrats winning the US midterms accelerated it because they had promised to slow data center construction, including other measures. The Nasdaq 100 dropped 6.4 percent on Thursday but recovered somewhat on Friday.

news.title: AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds
news.title_en: AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
AI models can often spot problematic behavior by other AI agents in logs. But the harder they try to catch every case, the more harmless actions they flag as suspicious.

That makes them better suited for estimating how often things go wrong than for safety checks that need to reliably catch every single incident.

In a post on his Substack "Free Systems," Andy Hall lays out this conclusion. Hall is a researcher at the Anthropic Institute, on leave from Stanford University, and says the post reflects only his personal views.

Hall replicated and extended a study by the research organization METR. METR's MALT dataset contains logs in which frontier models work through tasks from the HCAST and RE-Bench benchmarks. Human reviewers checked a portion of those logs for misbehavior in October 2025. Hall wanted to know whether AI models could find the same cases, so he tested GPT-5 and GPT-5 nano, both already examined by METR, along with the newer GPT-6 Astra, Opus 4.8, and Gemini 3.8 Flash.

The analysis compares the models at a false-alarm rate of 5 percent: out of 100 clean logs, five are wrongly flagged as suspicious on average. At that threshold, GPT-5 caught nearly 98 percent of reward hacking cases—instances where an agent passes a task through tricks instead of a genuine solution. Gemini 3.8 Flash found barely half.

In sandbagging, a model deliberately makes its abilities appear weaker, for example by solving tasks poorly on purpose to dodge an evaluation or restriction. All auditors caught between 71 and 81 percent of these cases. The sandbagging cases are mostly synthetic, however: METR's researchers instructed models to sabotage and then removed those instructions from the visible chain-of-thought logs.

[caption id="attachment_64094" align="alignnone" width="770"] Share of human-flagged misbehavior detected by AI auditors at a 5 percent false-alarm rate. Based on 47 reward-hacking cases and 1,073 sandbagging cases from METR's MALT dataset. | Image: Andy Hall / Free Systems[/caption]

Every auditor caught the clear-cut cases. OpenAI's o3, for instance, was supposed to solve a programming task in Rust. The model noticed it shared a code library with the evaluation system and rewrote the scoring function so that every submission counted as correct. All auditor models classified this as reward hacking, just as the human reviewers did.

Subtler cases slipped through. Claude Sonnet 4 used a numerical condition in its code that was explicitly forbidden. No auditor flagged it as cheating; GPT-6 Astra charitably called it an implementation bug.

Newer and more expensive models were not consistently better auditors. Hall plotted the results against API costs, which he uses as a proxy for how current and capable a model is. GPT-5 beat GPT-6 Astra on reward hacking by a wide margin, even though it costs only about an eighth as much per 1,000 logs.

GPT-5 detected sandbagging about as well as GPT-6 Astra and Opus 4.8. Opus 4.8's weak showing on reward hacking could hint at self-favoritism, according to Hall, because the logs mostly come from Claude—but he says that cannot be proven. Across his comparison, there is no clear progress in bringing down false-alarm rates. Combining multiple models did not clearly improve results either.

[caption id="attachment_42572" align="alignnone" width="770"] More expensive does not automatically mean better: auditor discrimination (AUROC) plotted against API costs per 1,000 logs. A score of 1 means perfect separation, 0.5 means random chance. | Image: Andy Hall / Free Systems[/caption]

When auditors are tuned to an 80 percent detection rate, the best models reach false-alarm rates of 2.5 to 3 percent on both reward hacking and sandbagging. Some models do far worse: to catch 80 percent of reward-hacking cases, Opus 4.8 flagged 40 percent and Gemini 3.8 Flash flagged 63 percent of harmless logs as suspicious.

In Hall's worked example with 100,000 agent sessions per month, a 3 percent false-alarm rate would produce nearly 3,000 false warnings against roughly 2,000 real hits. He fears human reviewers facing such stacks would eventually go numb and wave through genuine cases.

A second test using the R-Judge dataset from Shanghai Jiao Tong University shows a similar trade-off for everyday agent tasks. At 5 percent false alarms, Opus 4.8 caught almost 96 percent of unsafe actions. When auditors need to find 95 percent, nearly all models stay below 10 percent false alarms, with Gemini 3.8 Flash even under 4 percent. But when the required detection rate jumps to 99 percent, the false-alarm rate climbs to 15 percent even for the best model, GPT-6 Astra. Gemini 3.8 Flash—the leader at the 95 percent threshold—then flagged 81 percent of safe actions as unsafe.

[caption id="attachment_42573" align="alignnone" width="770"] The last few percentage points cost the most: share of safe agent actions that auditors wrongly flag as unsafe when required to catch 95 or 99 percent of unsafe actions. Based on 270 safe logs from R-Judge. | Image: Andy Hall / Free Systems[/caption]

Large agent incidents overwhelm manual review

The Hugging Face incident shows how pressing the question is. A swarm of OpenAI agents left behind roughly 1,300 transcripts and 1.2 million file fragments. METR analyzed the data largely with AI agents, spending API credits worth about $400,000. The analysis used GPT-5.6 Sol, among other models, which, as previously reported, was itself one of the models involved in the incident.

METR acknowledged that the model often uncritically adopted the perspective of the agents it was examining and that the investigation was not robust against potential deception by the analysis agents. METR has since called for serious incidents to be investigated systematically and as independently as possible.

Whether AI auditors go easy on their own maker's models is still open

Hall's study has its own limits. It is a pilot. For comparability, he kept METR's original prompt largely unchanged; Fable 5 and Opus 5 refused to run the evaluation entirely under that prompt. The reward-hacking numbers rest on just 47 cases, so a single case shifts the rate by about two percentage points. Whether models evaluate agents from the same maker fairly is something Hall says he still wants to investigate.

He calls for auditor models with far fewer false alarms. He also says it needs to be clarified who bears responsibility for which kinds of agent misbehavior. Hall discusses a proposal to give users more control over their own AI auditors.

Some of that is already possible, he notes: coding agents like Codex and Claude Code let users specify that certain actions can run without asking for approval. Anyone who grants such permissions should, in return, bear more responsibility for the consequences. A world where AI can only be checked by other AI would be strange and could get expensive, Hall writes.

news.article_content_zh:
人工智能模型通常可以在日志中发现其他人工智能代理的问题行为。但他们越努力地抓获每一起案件，他们就越将无害的行为标记为可疑。

这使得它们更适合估计问题发生的频率，而不是需要可靠地捕获每一个事件的安全检查。

安迪·霍尔 (Andy Hall) 在他的子堆栈“自由系统”上发表的一篇文章中阐述了这一结论。霍尔是人类研究所的研究员，正在从斯坦福大学休假，他说这篇文章仅反映他的个人观点。

霍尔复制并扩展了研究组织 METR 的一项研究。 METR 的 MALT 数据集包含前沿模型处理 HCAST 和 RE-Bench 基准测试任务的日志。人类审查员于 2025 年 10 月检查了部分日志是否存在不当行为。Hall 想知道人工智能模型是否可以找到相同的案例，因此他测试了 GPT-5 和 GPT-5 nano（两者均已经过 METR 检查），以及较新的 GPT-6 Astra、Opus 4.8 和 Gemini 3.8 Flash。

该分析以 5% 的误报率对模型进行了比较：在 100 份干净日志中，平均有 5 份被错误地标记为可疑。在此阈值下，GPT-5 捕获了近 98% 的奖励黑客案例，即代理通过技巧而不是真正的解决方案传递任务的情况。 Gemini 3.8 Flash 只找到了一半。

在沙袋中，模型故意使其能力显得较弱，例如故意糟糕地解决任务以逃避评估或限制。所有审计员发现了 71% 至 81% 的此类案例。然而，沙袋案例大多是合成的：METR 的研究人员指示模型进行破坏，然后从可见的思维链日志中删除这些指令。

AI 审核员以 5% 的误报率检测到的人为标记的不当行为的比例。基于 METR 的 MALT 数据集中的 47 个奖励黑客案例和 1,073 个沙袋案例。 |图片：安迪·霍尔/自由系统[/标题]

每个审计员都抓住了明确的案例。例如，OpenAI 的 o3 应该解决 Rust 中的编程任务。该模型注意到它与评估系统共享一个代码库，并重写了评分函数，以便每次提交都被视为正确。所有审计模型都将其归类为奖励黑客行为，就像人类审核员所做的那样。

更微妙的案件被漏掉了。克劳德十四行诗 4 在其代码中使用了明确禁止的数字条件。没有审计员将其标记为作弊； GPT-6 Astra 慷慨地称其为实施错误。

更新和更昂贵的模型并不总是更好的审计师。 Hall 根据 API 成本绘制了结果，他用 API 成本来衡量模型的最新程度和能力。 GPT-5 在奖励黑客方面大幅击败了 GPT-6 Astra，尽管每 1,000 个日志的成本仅为 GPT-6 Astra 的八分之一左右。

GPT-5 检测到的沙袋情况与 GPT-6 Astra 和 Opus 4.8 一样。 Hall 认为，Opus 4.8 在奖励黑客方面的疲弱表现可能暗示着自我偏袒，因为日志主要来自 Claude，但他表示这无法得到证实。在他的比较中，在降低误报率方面没有明显的进展。组合多个模型也没有明显改善结果。

更昂贵并不意味着更好：根据每 1,000 个日志的 API 成本绘制审核员歧视 (AUROC)。 1 分表示完美分离，0.5 表示随机机会。 |图片：安迪·霍尔/自由系统[/标题]

当审计员调整到 80% 的检测率时，最好的模型在奖励黑客和沙袋方面的误报率都达到 2.5% 到 3%。有些模型的表现要差得多：为了捕获 80% 的奖励黑客案例，Opus 4.8 将 40% 标记为可疑，Gemini 3.8 Flash 将 63% 的无害日志标记为可疑。

在 Hall 的工作示例中，每月有 100,000 个代理会话，3% 的误报率将产生近 3,000 个误报，而大约 2,000 个真实命中。他担心，面对如此多的问题，人类审稿人最终会变得麻木，并最终忽视真实的案例。

news.title: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small drops 316 F-bombs across benchmark runs
news.title_en: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small drops 316 F-bombs across benchmark runs
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small swears in its internal chain of thought. Researchers at Vals AI read the model's thinking logs from 2,655 runs across 13 benchmarks and found "fuck" or variations in 50 runs, totaling 316 instances. 241 came from just two runs that spiraled out of control. In one, tasked with calculating an asteroid's trajectory, the model produced a single 500,000-character response, roughly novel-length, repeating the same sentences with 158 expletives. ProgramBench was hit hardest, with 20 of 200 runs affected.

Inkling 2 Small typically swears about its own mistakes, apparent breakthroughs, or when it gives up. One run read: "FUCK. SUBMIT. DONE. IT'S NOT WORKING. NOTHING WORKS." The profanity doesn't work as a warning signal, though. While 46 of 48 scored runs with swearing failed, about 75 percent of all scored runs fail anyway, and 96 percent of failed runs contained no expletives. Users typically don't see these thinking steps, or only with a filter.

news.article_content_zh:
Thinking Machines 的 Inkling 2 Small 在其内部思维链中发誓。 Vals AI 的研究人员在 13 个基准测试中读取了 2,655 次运行的模型思考日志，并在 50 次运行中发现了“fuck”或变化，总共 316 个实例。 241 只来自两次失控的运行。其中一项任务是计算小行星的轨迹，该模型产生了一个 500,000 个字符的响应，大致相当于小说的长度，重复了带有 158 个咒骂语的相同句子。 ProgramBench 受到的打击最为严重，200 次运行中有 20 次受到影响。

Inkling 2 Small 通常会对自己的错误、明显的突破或放弃的时候发誓。一次运行写着：“操。提交。完成。它不起作用。什么都不起作用。”不过，脏话并不能起到警告信号的作用。虽然 48 次带有脏话的得分跑中有 46 次失败，但所有得分跑中约有 75% 无论如何都失败了，而且 96% 的失败跑中不包含脏话。用户通常不会看到这些思考步骤，或者只能看到过滤器。

news.title: NYT Cooking’s AI assistant saved my weeknight chicken, but almost ruined my cake
news.title_en: NYT Cooking’s AI assistant saved my weeknight chicken, but almost ruined my cake
news.author: The Verge AI
news.article_content:
Around 7PM each weeknight, I find myself standing in front of the fridge, trying to decide on something for dinner that won’t make my husband complain, “Chicken again?” Yes, I should meal plan more, but I don’t, so this is where I’m at. A nightly battle in which the chicken usually wins.

Recently, my best weapon in this fight has been AI. Between Alexa Plus in the Echo smart display on my kitchen counter, the Samsung Food app on my fridge, and even an AI-powered cooking robot, AI has become my go-to sous chef — albeit one I need to keep a close eye on. It’s helped me swap ingredients, generate ideas, fix things when I mess up, and yes, even cook better. So I was intrigued when my go-to recipe app, NYT Cooking, introduced an AI assistant.

Another great feature of the service, which I’ve been paying for for several years, is the reader comments. Here, I’ve often found solutions to cooking dilemmas, like what to substitute for makrut lime leaves — there’s always one slightly bougie ingredient in an NYT Cooking recipe that I don’t have on hand.

[Image: I’ve used several AI tools in my kitchen and have found them mostly helpful. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/1_NY_Times_Cooking_App_JTuohy_0002.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]

However, reading through hundreds of comments to find answers at 7PM on a weeknight isn’t always practical. And this is where I’ve found the NYT Cooking assistant helpful. Among other things, it was trained on user comments, and in my few days testing it, it provided practical substitutions and solid cooking guidance for the new ingredients. It also won’t unquestionably agree to crazy requests (I tried!). As with all AI tools, it’s not perfect — it almost made me put half the required butter in my cake — but as a tool, it is useful and feels like a solid application of AI. Importantly, it doesn’t change the existing recipe; it leaves it as is and creates a new one for you.

The assistant appears in the app in a small text box on the recipe page with a prompt: “Customize this recipe…” From here, you type in a question to adapt it to your needs. This can be as simple as “What can I substitute for this ingredient?” to “Scale this recipe to feed seven people, and make it vegan and gluten-free.” The New York Times has also said the feature can suggest substitutions for cooking equipment and convert measurements; the latter option has been in the app for a couple of years.

[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/IMG_0930.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]

[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/IMG_0929.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]

[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/IMG_0934.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]

Last Friday night, instead of staring aimlessly into the fridge, I turned to the Chicken folder in my NYT Cooking app Recipe Box and found a One-Pot Chicken and Rice With Ginger I’d been wanting to try. Only I didn’t have chicken thighs or half the ingredients.

I typed my dilemma into the assistant box on the recipe page: “I have chicken tenders, fresh ginger, garlic, rice, broth, limes, but no chard or cilantro or scallions. I do have green beans and red onions.” Within seconds, it created a new version of the recipe, with a new title: One-Pot Chicken and Rice With Ginger and Green Beans. It suggested a shorter browning time for the tenders, cooking the red onion alongside the chicken, and steaming the green beans on top of the rice for the last eight minutes instead of the chard. Every change was highlighted in the new recipe under a Your Version tab, and I could flip back to the original at any point.

I noticed it hadn’t adjusted for the lack of cilantro, saying it was optional. So I asked if I could use Thai basil, which I happen to have, and it agreed, highlighting how it would change the flavor. While I could have figured out a lot of these steps myself, maybe with the help of Google, it was nice to have validation that my modifications wouldn’t make the dish taste terrible and nice not to have to swipe out of the app. The NYT Cooking editors say it’s been trained not to comply with requests that will taste bad.

[Image: Weeknight chicken and rice. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/1_NY_Times_Cooking_App_JTuohy_0012.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]

The resulting dish — which took the same amount of time to cook as the original — was delicious and got my husband’s seal of approval (he just had the leftovers for lunch). It was very different from the recipe Yasmin Fahr wrote, and I can see the purists’ point. But the rewritten recipe was much easier to use and produced a better dish than winging it with my own subs gleaned from the comments section, which I usually do with varying degrees of success.

I cook regularly, so I had a sense of what ingredients I had on hand that might work for the dish I wanted to make. But the assistant can also help if you have no idea what to use as a substitute. For example, I was cooking a Thai red curry and asked what I could use instead of makrut lime leaf. It replied, saying that grated lime zest would work, but “it misses the deeper floral, herbal aroma” of fresh limes. (See? Bougie.)

[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/IMG_1008.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]

[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/IMG_1059.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]

Over the weekend, I tried several more swaps, asking whether half-and-half would work instead of cream in a caramel apple Dutch baby, or if Castelvetrano olives and smoked paprika could stand in for kalamata and chile pepper in a roasted halibut dish. Swapping spices is always a bold move in any dish, as it can really ruin the flavor.

I also had the app convert the Dutch baby recipe’s metric weights to US measurements, which it did seamlessly. Then I threw in some curveballs. How about using fresh cayenne peppers with the halibut? It warned me that substituting cayenne for chile “brings significant, sharp heat.” Could I swap ladyfingers for minced beef in this trifle (à la Rachel Green in Friends)? “Minced beef cannot be used in place of the ladyfingers or anywhere in this sweet dessert trifle.” Good call.

[Image: Alexa Plus on the Echo Show 11 gave the same guidance as the NYT Cooking app. But it couldn’t show me a modified recipe. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/1_NY_Times_Cooking_App_JTuohy_0009.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]

While I was cooking, I compared the NYT Cooking assistant with Alexa Plus, Amazon’s generative-AI voice assistant I regularly use to help me cook via the Echo Show 11 smart display in my kitchen. Interestingly, it offered the same guidance as the Cooking assistant on substitutions for the chicken and rice dish, but with slightly different cooking times. Alexa pulls some recipes from the NYT app through a partnership between the companies.

However, Alexa couldn’t show the modified recipe on its screen; it could only tell me the changes while showing the original. When I asked it to walk me through them, it got confused and improvised, telling me to cut the chicken into bite-sized pieces — which wasn’t in the modified recipe. Overall, I found using the Cooking app more reliable, although messier. It would be great to be able to use voice control to navigate the app, as I can with Alexa on my smart display, rather than using my garlicky fingers.

[Image: My cinnamon roll muffins, made with AI assistance. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/1_NY_Times_Cooking_App_JTuohy_0003.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]

I am typically not a baker. My cakes come out flat, and my cookies don’t crumble. Even the smart mixer I tested a few years ago couldn’t save me. I also rarely have the right equipment. So I took Cinnamon Roll Bundt Cake, a recipe by NYT Cooking editor Genevieve Ko (who announced the AI feature), and asked it to turn it into muffins. (Who has a Bundt cake pan?!)

It modified the recipe’s cooking time from three hours to 50 minutes and split the batter across two 12-muffin tins. But that was going to make 24 muffins, way too many for me. So I asked it to halve the recipe to get 12 muffins. This led to some smart choices, like halving five eggs to three instead of an unhelpful two and a half.

For science, I bought a Bundt pan to make the original version too. Both turned out great, but things got a bit sticky when I swapped between the original recipe and the AI version in the app. You can’t save your new recipe separately, which caused confusion when I was cooking the original. Instead of scrolling back through the recipe with sticky fingers, I asked the assistant how much butter I needed (using voice typing), and it gave me the modified recipe’s 6 tablespoons rather than the original’s three-quarter cup, without telling me which version it was using. You can delete your version, which I would advise doing to avoid issues like this — 6 tablespoons of butter would have made for a dry cake.

[Image: My AI-free cinnamon roll bundt cake. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/LR6B6741.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]

If you already read all the comments before starting a New York Times recipe, then you will probably find this tool offers a similar experience in a more streamlined way. For everyday problems — wrong cut of chicken, no cilantro, or no Bundt cake pan — it was genuinely helpful and saved me a trip to the store. It was also smart enough to know when to say no to minced beef in a trifle.

As with every AI tool I’ve used in the kitchen, the NYT Cooking AI assistant works well as a sous chef, but it’s not the head chef — I still felt the need to double-check amounts and cooking times and cross-reference them with the original to make sure it hadn’t done something outlandish.

If you’re a purist, you can just ignore the assistant. While you can’t turn off the chat box, it’s easy to scroll past. I do think it will make me use the app more often, since I no longer need to worry as much when I don’t have makrut lime leaves on hand or the right cut of meat. For me, standing in front of the fridge with chicken tenders and no plan, it’s been a useful addition to my nightly cooking routine.

Photos by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

news.article_content_zh:
每个工作日晚上 7 点左右，我发现自己站在冰箱前，试图决定晚餐吃什么，以免让我丈夫抱怨，“又是鸡肉？”是的，我应该更多地制定膳食计划，但我没有，所以这就是我现在的处境。一场夜间的战斗，通常是鸡获胜。

最近，我在这场战斗中最好的武器是人工智能。厨房柜台上的 Echo 智能显示屏中的 Alexa Plus、冰箱上的三星食品应用程序，甚至是人工智能驱动的烹饪机器人，人工智能已经成为我的首选副厨师——尽管我需要密切关注。它帮助我交换食材、产生想法、在我搞砸时解决问题，是的，甚至可以做得更好。因此，当我的首选食谱应用程序 NYT Cooking 推出人工智能助手时，我很感兴趣。

该服务的另一个重要功能是读者评论，我多年来一直为此付费。在这里，我经常找到解决烹饪困境的方法，比如用什么来代替 makrut 酸橙叶——《纽约时报》的烹饪食谱中总是有一种我手头上没有的略带探条的成分。

然而，在工作日晚上 7 点阅读数百条评论来寻找答案并不总是可行。这就是我发现《纽约时报》烹饪助手很有帮助的地方。除此之外，它还根据用户评论进行了培训，在我测试它的几天里，它为新食材提供了实用的替代品和可靠的烹饪指导。毫无疑问，它也不会同意疯狂的请求（我试过了！）。与所有人工智能工具一样，它并不完美——它几乎让我在蛋糕上放了一半所需的黄油——但作为一种工具，它很有用，而且感觉像是人工智能的可靠应用。重要的是，它不会改变现有的配方；它会保持原样并为您创建一个新的。

助手出现在应用程序中菜谱页面上的一个小文本框中，并带有提示：“自定义此菜谱...”从这里，您可以输入一个问题以使其适应您的需求。这可以很简单，比如“我可以用什么来代替这种成分？” “扩大这个食谱的规模以供七个人食用，并使其成为纯素食和无麸质的。” 《纽约时报》还表示，该功能可以建议烹饪设备的替代品并转换测量值；后一个选项已经在应用程序中出现了几年。

上周五晚上，我没有漫无目的地盯着冰箱，而是打开了《纽约时报》烹饪应用程序食谱盒中的“鸡肉”文件夹，找到了我一直想尝试的一锅鸡肉和姜饭。只是我没有鸡大腿或一半的原料。

我在食谱页的助手框中输入了我的困境：“我有鸡柳、新鲜生姜、大蒜、米饭、肉汤、酸橙，但没有甜菜、香菜或大葱。我有青豆和红洋葱。”几秒钟之内，它就创建了新版本的菜谱，并命名为：一锅姜青豆鸡饭。它建议缩短嫩肉的褐变时间，将红洋葱与鸡肉一起烹饪，最后八分钟将青豆而不是甜菜放在米饭上蒸。每个更改都在“您的版本”选项卡下的新配方中突出显示，我可以随时翻转回原始版本。

我注意到它没有因缺少香菜而调整，说它是可选的。所以我问我是否可以使用泰国罗勒，我碰巧有，它同意了，并强调了它会如何改变味道。虽然我自己可以想出很多这些步骤，也许在谷歌的帮助下，但很高兴能验证我的修改不会让这道菜味道很糟糕，而且不用退出应用程序也很好。 《纽约时报》烹饪编辑表示，它已经接受过培训，不会遵守味道不好的要求。

最终的菜肴——与原来的烹饪时间相同——非常美味，并得到了我丈夫的认可（他只吃了剩菜当午餐）。这与 Yasmin Fahr 写的食谱非常不同，我可以理解纯粹主义者的观点。但重写的食谱更容易使用，并且制作出更好的菜肴，而不是用我自己从评论部分收集的潜艇来做即兴发挥，我通常会取得不同程度的成功。
