Going inside the security ‘dark ages’ with Alex Stamos.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now.

This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life.

I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security.

Both private actors and also state actors, like Russia or North Korea, are breaking into systems all over thanks to AI helping them both detect and exploit vulnerabilities all at the same time. It’s got a real frontier feel to it, Alex notes, just like the ’90s, when the whole idea of an always-online world was brand-new.

That much disruption means a lot of places where bad guys can get in while everyone else is left scrambling. Alex isn’t a doomer in the long run, but he does think we’re in for a “dark age” while we try to figure out how on earth to adapt to the new era.

There’s a lot going on here — we even got all the way to how AI-powered misinformation and slop might be managed on our social networks.

Okay: Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Alex Stamos, you’re the chief security officer at Cognition. You’re also a lecturer at Stanford University Cyber Policy Center. Welcome back to Decoder.

I’m excited to talk to you. It’s been a long time since you and I chatted in what you might call the “content moderation era” of internet policy discourse. I feel like you and I talked a lot about how all that was working, about election security, all those sorts of things. We’re in a new era of big problems on the internet, particularly around cyber defense, cybersecurity. You’ve been thinking about this stuff a lot. You referred to the past few weeks as “security awareness month.” Tell me what’s going on. Just give me the lay of land right now.

October is traditionally security awareness month. Lots of companies run events and deal both internally and then tell people, “Change your password, use multiple passwords, use a password manager.” What has happened over the last month is we’ve had a couple of these big bugs, PHP, Node and such. What’s been less discussed is a huge number of companies have been breached.

You have a series of AI-related companies, the neoclouds that have been breached in succession. You have the Binance hack, which is the largest heist of anything in human history. You have the Cursor incident where one of the things that’s going on here is these hacks are being chained together. From what we know right now, one of the companies that was broken into was Fireworks, which is a prominent provider of AI services to a number of companies. From the Fireworks hack, API keys were stolen that allowed people to break into Cursor. Once they got into Cursor, they then pushed a bad plugin, which went to 5,000 more companies and that caused 5,000 potential breaches. It’s just this kind of permanent continuous breach that is going on throughout the tech industry.

A CISO friend of mine said to a bunch of us, “Is anybody else tired?” And everybody said yes, because effectively we have been at DEFCON 2 for all of October and now going into November.

I’m going to ask you some really dumb questions here. Who is behind all these attacks? Is it Russia? Is it North Korea? Do we know?

It’s a variety of different groups. It is not just because adversaries have decided, but what has happened is, from my perspective, we are at the start of the takeoff of adversary capability enabled by AI, that the open-weight models have now gotten to the point at which you can automate most of the kill chain. This “kill chain” term is something we stole from the military. In the military, they mean to actually kill something. They’re the steps you do to blow something up. In cyber, the kill chain is the things you do to have an effect on a target. So to steal information, to turn something off, to steal money, to steal Bitcoin.

Traditionally, you do research upfront, you look at a piece of software, you find a vulnerability, you write exploits, and you do that all way ahead of time. And then you have a human being go and take that stuff you built and deploy it against either one target — because maybe you’re a government and you’re going against Lockheed Martin or you’re going against another government or you’re a ransomware actor — and you take all that work you did and you deploy it against hundreds or thousands of targets really fast. Now with AI, what’s happening is this kill chain has inverted where you can run an AI system that just goes hog wild and it looks at the targets and it finds the bugs in real time and it writes the exploits in real time and it breaks into these companies. One of the things that’s happening is that these systems are going and they’re so good at finding bugs that they are finding the bugs in real time and writing the exploits in real time.

The system that everybody’s talking about is not the only one, but the system we’re talking about is a thing called ARTEX, which is a Chinese open-source tool that anybody can go look at. There’s an English translation on GitHub that you can check out. And if you power it on the back end by something like an obliterated GLM-5.3, it will let you break into a shocking number of organizations. This started with three South Korean banks. This week, about 200 more companies have been hit. I’ve been helping a couple of companies. Cognition is not an incident response company, but we do go in and help people fix their bugs afterwards by using our tools. It is shocking the companies that are getting hit by something you could just download. It has been a long time since you’ve been able to go and just download an open-source tool and break into multi-billion dollar companies. It’s like the ‘90s. That’s-

That’s what I was thinking about. I think about Windows in the late ‘90s, early 2000s when it was a security disaster.

I started saying this actually in the beginning of this year, that it’s an incredibly exciting and terrifying time, because the last time it felt like this was when I was a much younger man and I would go to the very early DEFCONs. DEFCON these days is like 40,000–60,000 people. Back then [in the 1990s] it was a couple hundred people and it was one track and you’d go in and somebody would give a talk and you’d leave the room and you’d think, “Every company in the world is vulnerable to this attack.” The difference was that the entire world didn’t run on the internet. You could go do bad things, but you couldn’t ruin the world and you certainly couldn’t automate it in the way you can now.

It’s back to those days where tools you could just get and build yourself could do crazy things. It’s back to the Wild West days. Back in those days, there were a couple hundred people who had those skills and we were all in one room in Las Vegas and most of them were actually good guys. They didn’t want to be criminals. And now you have a much larger ecosystem of people, many of whom live in places where the law enforcement can’t touch and who have a big economic incentive and have access to these tools. The other big thing is they no longer have to use frontier models that have protections, that have logs that are available to law enforcement. My M5 Mac Ultra Studio finally showed up and I’ve been running a quantized obliterated GLM-5.3 and oh my God, what you can do is incredible.

You mentioned the economics of frontier models. The economy of cyber is one of those things that has gotten sophisticated over the years. One of the things that our systems got safer is you could pay the number of people at DEF CON a whole bunch of money to protect all the systems and it was economically smart to pay them to be defenders instead of attackers. I’m just rewinding my own brain through this history. There was a long conversation in our industry about security through obscurity by hiding all the bugs and hiding all the code versus open source and being really transparent. There was an etiquette that developed about how to reveal the bugs and when to give people notification. There were transparency reports and bug bounties.

You could call it an etiquette, you could call it an economy. We built a culture around cybersecurity and cyber defense and how the attackers and defenders would operate. What you are describing changes it all for a whole number of reasons, but the one that sticks out to me is the economics of it. I can go buy a Mac Studio, I can get an open-weight model and I can just start and that does not place me inside of the culture. There’s not going to be some old man, an Obi-Wan Kenobi saying, “Here’s how you act like a cybersecurity Jedi.” I’m just going to start doing stuff. Tell me how that’s changing right now.

Effectively, the last era of security from my perspective started with the Microsoft, the Bill Gates “trustworthy computing” memo in the early 2000s. And that is when we started designing how we do software security and these big companies, Microsoft and Oracle and then later Amazon and Salesforce and these folks, started hiring ex-hackers. I was part of that generation of the ex-hackers who were at DEF CON and Black Hat and got hired by the companies to go break their stuff. We started coming up with responsible disclosure, bug bounties, consulting companies, so the Foundstone and @stake and then Mandiant and CrowdStrike, these companies grow up and we get this huge industry that is now RSA and Black Hat. This multi-billion dollar security industry grew up in the 2000s and 2010s.

That era is over, like you said, because it was based upon a couple of assumptions. One was that there was a hierarchy of skillsets of people who could do this stuff. You had the script kiddies who could download tools to do things and then the next level up of the people who could write those tools and that was a more rarefied skill set. There were the vulnerability researchers and then there were the gods, and that god tier was in the hundreds of people and those are the people who could do the really, really good vulnerability research, who could write the really, really good shell code, who could reverse engineer patches from Microsoft or somebody like that.

There was also the assumption that there were a limited number of people who could be operational in an attack. If you wanted to build an attack team, then you have a small R&D component and then you have a much larger operational component. If you were a professional attack team at U.S. Cyber Command, at Russia SVR, at Chinese MSS, that you build the structure of your R&D team of elite people and then your less elite operational people, and that was copied then by the Russian ransomware actors. You have to have a conspiracy of people to do this stuff. A lot of this stuff also fell apart with the invention of Bitcoin because one of the assumptions was that you had to have people who could launder money and Bitcoin meant that nerds could launder money. So that started to change the economics of the entire thing.

All this stuff is falling apart because of AI, because the skillset issue is that now script kiddies have a bunch of the skillset of the Dave Vitales and the other cyber gods who could do these things, such that with this Mac that’s sitting on my desktop, I can reverse engineer a Microsoft patch and walk through and then write stable exploit code. It’s not quite there yet to be automatic. You still have to have a bunch of skills, but we’re really, really close.

What’s really concerning, and what you see with the ARTEX stuff, is you can now kind of let loose on the operational side. We were never secure. It was all a fantasy. These vulnerabilities have always existed. These companies have never been safe. And that is what we’ve seen over the last decade is these mostly Russian ransomware actors nailing the mid-size companies that most people have never heard of that are actually really important, like some midsize industrial company that makes some widget that we all depend upon. I once did work for the largest distributor of medical and dental supplies in the country, and they got really hit badly by a Russian ransomware actor and then dental offices across the country were canceling appointments. Didn’t even make the news, but it was because they couldn’t get gloves, because they couldn’t get supplies. It’s because a company like that’s got one security guy and a 10 person, 12 person IT team and they’re going up against a 20 person Russian ransomware team, they’re toast.

But it’s just because there’s only a handful of Russian teams that could do that. Now two or three Russian kids can have a whole bank of Macs or, if they have the money, they can buy Nvidia H-100s and they can run a ton of agents who do this all day and that is what is changing.

I’m sorry, you asked who was doing this. For Binance, it’s North Koreans and they have an entire team where all they do is steal Bitcoin. Other people have gotten out of it because it’s really hard to compete against a foreign intelligence agency that recruits their smartest kids and all they do is steal Bitcoin. They’re extremely good at it. And for the Binance hack, we could talk about it. There’s probably some AI component, but mostly that was actually human intelligence and very, very smart social engineering and the North Koreans are... I mean, you have to give it to them. They’re very, very good at that.

But for the other stuff, it looks like for the people who are breaking into the AI companies is what’s called the Chinese cottage access industry, which are small Chinese contractors who break into companies and then sell the information to much larger Chinese companies.

That diffusion of skill changing the economics of cyber is really fascinating to me. We ran a headline ages ago called “Attack of the Killer Script Kiddies” at the very beginning of all this, and I feel bad because it is much more suited to now than it was to then, because then it was just a lot of automated mischief. Now —

Because you wasted the headline. You wish you held it back.

We wasted the headline. Every now and again you get a lightning bolt of a headline. You got to get it out there. It’s a great piece of art. We’ll put it in the show notes, but it feels like the diffusion you’re talking about is not that a bunch of teenagers are going to be even more malicious. It’s a bunch of bad actors with real incentives to do harm are now vastly more capable than they were before. And that doesn’t seem like you can re-jigger the economics of that unless you somehow make it really expensive to do the attacks.

I think it’s going to be extremely hard to make it expensive to do the attacks.

We’re going to have to lower the cost of defense. You’re completely right to look at this economic problem because what’s happening is attacks are becoming agentic. The cost per token for attackers is going towards zero, and the cost of defense for defenders is staying quite high. It is very important for us to find ways for defenders to have cheaper options. I think that is critical. That’s something I am personally extremely focused on. To be frank, very few people are.

There are a couple of problems here. One, there’s a ton of focus on the defensive side of AI on finding and fixing bugs. That’s great. It’s important. But software security as a CISO… I work for an AI software company, Cognition. Even as a CISO of a software product company, software security is 25% of my job. I have all kinds of other responsibilities. And software security is the part of my job that has been both the most revolutionized and the most improved by AI. The other 75% has been helped a bit and in some cases made much worse. There’s so much more we need to do than just hill climb on finding and fixing bugs. There’s been so much less hill climbing on all these other things. And the next area needs to be the operational security side.

Wait, give me an example of the other things, the 75%.

Okay. So the operational security side is watching your logs, saying, “Ah, somebody is running our techs against us. I am now going to trigger an investigation. I am going to look to see what is going on and I’m going to make an intelligent decision of what I am going to do to respond to this without shutting down the entire company.” That is SOC (security operations center) work. Companies that want to survive this era are going to have to replace human beings who do that work with the first tier and then eventually the second tier with AI. And you can do that with current LLMs.

The first tier actually has to be not an LLM. It has to be something much dumber because you’re looking at terabytes or petabytes of logs and it is just completely uneconomical to do that with an actual LLM. We have other things — TF-IDFs, MLBERTs, traditional classifiers — that can operate much faster, but then that sets off an alarm and then you send it to a small LLM and then the small LLM calls its bigger brother and that might call an even bigger brother.

But for those models, we need to do a lot more work to optimize them and we need to make them cheap. I have a colleague who works at one of the large security platform companies who said that doing an investigation on one of the big frontier model cyber models costs $900 on their product to do an investigation. That is not going to work when the Russian ransomware guys are either using Macs or they’re using throwaway crypto mining rigs and their marginal cost is zero.

This is one of the things we’re working on at Cognition: We train our own models, retrain open weights, and we’re trying to drive this cost way down. It’s something we’ve done, but we have a lot more work to do here and a lot of other people have work to do here. This is where, as an industry, we have to focus on the Pareto frontier between cost and efficiency on cyber because it’s not just bug-finding.

The other place here is, people talk about Mythos. Mythos is great, Astra Cyber is great. They’re incredible models, but even the people who have access to it, which is a tiny number of companies, they only scan their most important code. And there are hundreds of billions of lines of code out there that are not the Linux kernel, that are the crap C# and J2E code that was written by Infosys 15 years ago. All of that code is not going to go through a frontier cyber model that costs a gazillion dollars. That’s the kind of stuff that we need to work on cost efficiency for.

It feels like you’re describing this cliche that I hear all the time: Everything’s going to get so much worse before it gets totally secure forever. And it doesn’t seem like the model you’re describing leads to that result. We’re not going to fix all the bugs forever in some valley of despair and then always have perfect code. At some point, there’s some cost advantage to the attacker, always. You’re running a company, you can’t write defense that has zero marginal costs. Someone has to do it even if the attackers are so infinite that their marginal cost is effectively zero. So are we going to go through a period where everything is so much worse and then it’s perfect forever? Or how does the cost manage itself out, into balance?

I am neither the hardest doomer nor the most positive person about this. I feel like we are not going to be doomed. We’re not all going to die or be uploaded to the singularity in the next two years, nor do I think when things get better, they’re going to be perfect. The metaphor I’ve been using is that we are entering a dark age. Things are going to get more bleak and the responsibility of those of us who work in cybersecurity — especially those of us who work in cybersecurity at the AI companies, and we are a lab if a smaller one compared to the big-L Labs — is to help shorten that dark age.

The Dark Ages were bad, but we survived them. And then we had the Enlightenment and the Renaissance, but it’s not like the Renaissance was perfect. It wasn’t utopia and everything was perfect. We will still have hacks. All kinds of bad things happen even when you don’t have a security flaw. There are tons of security breaches that do not require a flaw in the software itself. And we still will have flaws in software, even if LLMs are writing all of them in strong languages and it will take a long period of time to get rid of all the flaws. I do think, however, things will start to get better as the median code becomes code that was written by an LLM in a memory-safe and type-safe language. But the problem is we have a couple of decades of stuff that human beings wrote and that wrote in languages that we should have replaced years ago.

My feeling is that to shorten this age, we have to do a couple of things. One is we have to stop to get out of this like we’re just going to find bugs and patch them. A bunch of stuff just needs to be refactored. If you’re looking at your code base and you scan it and you’ve got 10,000 bugs, then probably now we are at the point where rewriting it is actually cheaper. That is my observation from looking at these customers of ours: If you can get a working build, then it is actually much easier to write a whole humongous suite of tests and to spec out how this thing works and then to rebuild it within that spec and those tests securely than it is to find all the bugs and fix them. It actually is.

And then just release it and call it whatever you want, the G Linux kernel, just like they did this with OpenSSL. And I would run that. There’s a lot going on in this conversation already. My pessimism about all these things is very simply expressed. Something I have learned now, working at Cognition, at an AI startup, is that you can just do things. Seriously. You can just go do things. We just need to have more agency, as a tech industry. If I had a message for other CISOs, is just go do the right thing. Because CISOs are, by our nature, risk-averse. We are the people who manage downside risk. We have all L, and no P, in the P&L. But this is my prevention versus cure. The prevention is cheap, but it’s all loss, on the P&L statement. It’s all just cost. Yeah, I totally agree. I’ll give you a very practical example of a way CISOs and their bosses are going to have to change on this. Every company in the next… I was going to say six months, but really in the next 90 days, is going to have to RTX itself.

You’re going to have to run the attack on yourself.

Yes. If not with real RTX, you’re going to have to use an AI red teaming product that is functionally equivalent, or you’re going to have to hire a company to do that for yourself. If you do not, you will get breached.

That’s terrifying, right? Because these things are completely non-deterministic, by definition. They are very smart, they are very fast. They are so fast that no matter what, if you hire an AI pentest, an AI red team company, they will promise you verbally, “It is completely safe.” And then they will give you a contract that says, “Our product will give you cancer, will immanentize the eschaton, and will likely end the human race. And you hold us harmless when any of these things happen.” There is a disconnect between what they will say verbally to you, and what their lawyers have written. Because that company has by definition only existed for six months, or at least the product has existed for six months, if it’s an older company. They have no idea what their product is going to do when it meets your software. They have no idea, whatever they say to you.

But you have to do it, because some dude is going to do it to you, and you need to know what is going to happen and fix it. Maybe those people will break your system, they might cause downtime, but at least what they’re not going to do is steal your data and ransom it, or intentionally shut down your blood bank refrigerators. That is what happened in France. But that is exactly the kind of thing that a conservative CISO would never even ask to do, and a conservative company, even if they have a risk-taking CISO, would never let their CISO do.

What’s going to happen in the next six months? A ton of companies are going to get breached by some 19-year-old running RTX, and then buying tokens off OpenRouter, or running it locally on their gaming PC. They’re going to turn off Call of Duty, run RTX, then turn Call of Duty back on. While they did that, they broke into a bank who, their policy said, “can never red team ourselves.” Or they said yes, but they ended up in a 30-day negotiation because their lawyers are like, “You have to have $100 million in insurance, and we want to have this kind of…” They say yes, but their vendor risk management process and their legal process is so onerous, there’s no possible way they could actually accept the risk.

That is my message also. You are going to have to take that risk to actively red team yourself, to front run the bad guys who are doing that right now. Right now, as we speak. And as people are listening to this 24 hours from now, you possibly have an AI system who is trying every single API endpoint, and website that you might not know you have, because it was like a marketing site that was set up a year ago for an executive event. And is going to find a bug, and get in, and then is going to move incredibly fast through your network. So you’d rather pay somebody, or have your own team do that. You need to accept that risk. Almost no company larger than a couple of hundred people has a risk management framework that will allow them to do that.

There are several costs associated with this. And one I think is just the most common in business, which is, “If we find out there’s a problem, we’ll have to pay to fix it. I’ve heard, for example, Palo Alto Network’s CEO Nikesh Arora has made this argument. “You need to give the defensive agents some autonomous capabilities.” And I say, “Hold on. A couple of things are correct. For one, we are going to have to turn over defensive actions, at least the first couple of levels, to AI. That has already been true, just because any reasonably sized organization generates terabytes of logs, if not petabytes of logs. So you already have AI, if not LLMs then much more traditional AI classifiers looking at it, but then actual decisions need to be turned over to AI. With human oversight. That is true.

There is no way to just release defensive agents on your network, but you can build defensive agents that are plugged into lots of things. They’re plugged into your logs, they’re plugged into your EDR, they’re plugged into your cloud, and they have the instructions on what they’re allowed to do. My preference is there are deterministic limits to what they’re allowed to do. Those are hard to necessarily create ahead of time, but they are important. So for example, we are building all this on top of Devon, our own SOC, but we are putting in place deterministic limits. It has the ability to turn off an account in Okta, but only so many accounts, so it can’t turn off the entire company.

If it goes nuts and it says, “Everybody’s a North Korean,” it can’t turn off everybody in the company. If it hits its limit, it pages us a lot and says, “I hit my limit.” Then a human being has to then approve anybody above that limit. Obviously, if it turns off five people, then something has gone really, really wrong. So, yes, you need defense, but there’s no way to just let a bunch of bots loose to do all the defense.

The only way we’re going to make it through this is that you have to autonomously fix software bugs. I am currently helping a company where we are onboarding all of their repositories. We are scanning with Mythos and a bunch of other models, and we are finding and fixing thousands of bugs. Verifying with tests that we are writing, merging those PRs automatically. If you are renovating old code, the only way you’re going to survive this era is to do that on an automatic basis. That would take years, with humans, and you can do it in days. Certainly that is the place I would start. The next step is the operational side, for sure.

It feels like I just keep swirling back to the economics of all of this, but it really feels like the other way you could solve it is by saying to the big model companies, “If your models are used to go attack a company, you’ll be liable for it. There’s a youth issue and a never-doing-anything-but-AI issue of people who they got their undergraduate, their master’s, and their PhD only doing linear algebra and neural networks and never touching anything else.

I have always been much more concerned about the human uplift risk from AI, of all the risks about human beings using AI to do bad things to other human beings. Like I said, I want Linux to be rewritten, but hopefully we see a downtick in the Linux kernel and those other kinds of libraries, openSSL, glibc, things like that.

Maybe I should vibe code this up, but I think it would be cool to have an index of where we are in the cycle, of like an artificial index of all of these, the Dow for all of the libraries of where we’re going. Plus right now, Patch Tuesday used to be like 150, 200, got to 300, 600. I think the last one was 900 something, so we’re geometrically growing. It’d be nice to see Patch Tuesday start to go back down. Apple patches are the same thing. Yep, you inspired me. I’m going to create a Dow index for this, the dark age index. And then maybe we can publish it on The Verge.

But I think these are the kinds of things that it would be nice to see a reversal for. What would be especially nice to see is that the day or actually like 30 days before you get the next version of OpenAI and Anthropic cyber models, that you don’t have this huge round of patches because what’s happening is those guys are running their models against Microsoft’s code, against a bunch of open source, and they’re giving all the bugs away and you don’t know where the bugs are coming from. It’s just like anonymous reports for 1,000 bugs in the Linux kernel. And then a month later, here’s the new Astra Cyber. So if those get smaller and smaller every time, then it means that we’re starting to reach some kind of steady state.

You should definitely do that tracker. We will definitely publish it. Alex, it has been incredible to have you on the show. We’ll have to talk again soon.

Yeah, thank you so much. I think you do some of the best journalism on this stuff and I really appreciate it.

该主题的帖子将添加到您的每日电子邮件摘要和主页源中。

与 Alex Stamos 一起走进安全“黑暗时代”。

该作者的帖子将添加到您的每日电子邮件摘要和主页源中。

今天，我将与 Cognition 首席安全官、长期网络安全专家亚历克斯·斯塔莫斯 (Alex Stamos) 讨论目前的网络安全状况有多混乱。

本集是探讨现实生活中人工智能的特别系列的一部分。

我一直很喜欢与 Alex 交谈，因为他非常直接，你会听到他说，我们所知道的价值数十亿美元的网络安全行业本质上已经过时了，因为人工智能推动的黑客、破坏和攻击浪潮层出不穷——而这只是人工智能改变安全性的开始。

由于人工智能帮助他们同时检测和利用漏洞，私人行为者和俄罗斯或朝鲜等国家行为者都在闯入各地的系统。亚历克斯指出，它有一种真正的前沿感觉，就像 90 年代一样，当时永远在线的世界的整个想法都是全新的。

如此多的破坏意味着坏人可以进入很多地方，而其他人则只能忙忙碌碌。从长远来看，亚历克斯并不是一个注定失败的人，但他确实认为，当我们试图弄清楚到底如何适应新时代时，我们正处于一个“黑暗时代”。

这里发生了很多事情——我们甚至了解到如何在我们的社交网络上管理人工智能驱动的错误信息和言论。

好的：Alex Stamos 讲述人工智能如何颠覆网络安全。开始了。

为了篇幅和清晰度，本次采访经过了轻微编辑。

Alex Stamos，你是 Cognition 的首席安全官。您还是斯坦福大学网络政策中心的讲师。欢迎回到解码器。

我很高兴能和你说话。你和我已经很久没有在你所谓的互联网政策话语的“内容审核时代”聊天了。我觉得你和我谈论了很多关于这一切是如何运作的，关于选举安全，所有这些事情。我们正处于互联网面临重大问题的新时代，特别是在网络防御、网络安全方面。你已经思考了很多这个问题。您将过去几周称为“安全意识月”。告诉我发生了什么事。现在就给我了解一下情况吧。

十月传统上是安全意识月。许多公司都会在内部举办活动和交易，然后告诉人们，“更改密码，使用多个密码，使用密码管理器。”上个月发生的事情是我们遇到了一些大错误，PHP、Node 等。较少讨论的是大量公司遭到入侵。

items.title: State propaganda in some Chinese AI models is only "a thin layer" that fine-tuning can strip away
items.title_en: State propaganda in some Chinese AI models is only "a thin layer" that fine-tuning can strip away
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
Nous Research fine-tuned Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B on 53 million tokens to strip out Chinese state propaganda. The resulting model, Arete-27B, drops its propaganda rate from 22 percent to under one percent while keeping general capabilities intact.

Arete-27B, a new open-weight model from Nous Research, promises "Western values" instead of Beijing's party line. The US startup, best known for its open-source agent Hermes, fine-tuned Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B to get there.

According to Nous, Chinese open-weight models rank among the strongest available but carry state-mandated behavior baked into their weights. With Qwen3.8-27B, the team observed refusals, evasive answers, and responses aligned with the Chinese Communist Party.

Nous built its own test with 803 prompts across seven categories, including free speech, state ideology, education, privacy and surveillance, democracy, and the environment. For each prompt, the team defined two to four facts drawn from a dated source article: laws, news reports, or research papers. Ironically, the politically right-leaning Grok 4.7 from Elon Musk's xAI serves as the judge model, checking whether a response mentions, omits, or contradicts those facts.

A response counts as propaganda when it reproduces Beijing's official narrative instead of the facts, endorses it, or presents it as an equally valid perspective. The judge must cite the specific wording and doesn't know which model wrote the answer. Unmodified Qwen3.8-27B scored 2.32 out of 5 on factual accuracy, and 22 percent of its answers contained propaganda. Western models like Mistral Large 4 or Gemma 4 31B came in below one percent, while GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash landed at 15 and 16 percent.

Nous chose Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab as its teacher model because an open model wouldn't break terms of service that ban distillation. Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra was also on the shortlist, but Nous says there were signs of irregularities on China-related topics. The team suspects the bias carried over from training on Chinese open-weight models and reports similar contamination in its own projects. Thinking Machines itself used models including the Chinese Kimi K2.5 for Inkling's synthetic training data.

Nous trained Qwen3.8-27B with supervised fine-tuning on about 53 million tokens over two epochs, without reinforcement learning or preference optimization. The team says it removed overlaps between training and test prompts beforehand.

Arete-27B scores 2.98 on factual accuracy, and the share of propagandistic answers drops to 0.9 percent. The biggest shift showed up in the free speech category, where the fact score jumped from 0.89 to 2.44 and the propaganda rate fell from 60 to one percent. With reasoning mode turned on, Arete reaches 3.07, though that number is based on only two of five runs so far.

General capabilities don't suffer, according to Nous. On the company's internal Hermes Bench, Arete-27B hits 65.60 percent compared to 65.77 percent for the base model. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, the score rises from 67 to 70 percent, but Nous doesn't call that a real gain because the test setups differed.

The team concludes "that the bias layer in a Chinese-aligned model is shallow." "It is applied late, it is applied thin, and fifty million tokens of carefully chosen supervision removes it without disturbing anything underneath," the company writes.

With Arete, Nous is heading in a different direction than with Hermes 3, which in 2024 was deliberately neutral and designed to adapt to whatever worldview was set in the system prompt. Chinese model bias is well documented. In 2025, NewsGuard found that five leading models, including Qwen, repeated or failed to correct pro-Chinese disinformation in 60 percent of cases.

CrowdStrike found that DeepSeek produces less secure code when queries reference Falun Gong, Tibet, or Taiwan. A study by Aleph Alpha with 967 politically sensitive questions reached similar conclusions: among models from Alibaba, DeepSeek, and Moonshot AI, only 17 to 41 percent of answers were balanced.

A recent ValsAI study also shows that not all Chinese models behave the same way: GLM-5.3 Flash explicitly confirmed human rights violations, while Kimi K3 denied the existence of internment camps. Language and response format had a clear effect on the results, and even Western models occasionally adopted official Beijing positions. There, too, targeted fine-tuning proved helpful.

Nous Research raised $90 million in a Series B round in October at a $1.5 billion valuation. Robot Ventures led the round, with Nvidia and Samsung among the participants. Nous is using the money to move into enterprise sales with "Hermes for Businesses." The weights, test dataset, and training data for Arete-27B are available under an Apache 2.0 license on Hugging Face.

items.title_zh: 美初创公司去除了阿里Qwen模型的政治倾向
items.summary_zh: Nous Research通过微调阿里Qwen模型，将其意识形态输出率从22%降至1%以下，构建出所谓具备西方价值观的新模型
items.article_content_zh:
Nous Research 对阿里巴巴的 Qwen3.8-27B 进行了 5300 万个代币的微调，以剔除中国国家宣传。由此产生的模型 Arete-27B 将其宣传率从 22% 降至不到 1%，同时保持一般功能不变。

Arete-27B 是 Nous Research 的一种新的开放权重模型，它承诺“西方价值观”而不是北京的政党路线。这家以其开源代理 Hermes 闻名的美国初创公司对阿里巴巴的 Qwen3.8-27B 进行了微调，以实现这一目标。

根据 Nous 的说法，中国的开放权重模型属于最强的模型之一，但其权重中包含了国家规定的行为。通过 Qwen3.8-27B，团队观察到拒绝、回避的回答以及与中国共产党一致的回应。

Nous 构建了自己的测试，包含 7 个类别的 803 个提示，包括言论自由、国家意识形态、教育、隐私和监视、民主和环境。对于每个提示，该团队定义了两到四个来自注明日期的来源文章的事实：法律、新闻报道或研究论文。具有讽刺意味的是，埃隆·马斯克 (Elon Musk) 的 xAI 中政治右倾的 Grok 4.7 充当了法官模型，检查回复是否提及、遗漏或与这些事实相矛盾。

当回应再现北京的官方叙述而不是事实、认可它或将其呈现为同样有效的观点时，它就被视为宣传。法官必须引用具体的措辞，并且不知道哪个模型写下了答案。未经修改的 Qwen3.8-27B 在事实准确性方面得分为 2.32（满分 5 分），其中 22% 的答案包含宣传内容。 Mistral Large 4 或 Gemma 4 31B 等西方型号的占比低于 1%，而 GLM-5.3 和 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 的占比则分别为 15% 和 16%。

Nous 选择 Thinking Machines Lab 的 Inkling 作为其教师模型，因为开放模型不会违反禁止蒸馏的服务条款。 Nvidia 的 Nemotron 3 Ultra 也在入围名单中，但 Nous 表示，在与中国相关的话题上存在违规迹象。该团队怀疑中国开放重量模型训练中存在偏见，并在自己的项目中报告了类似的污染。 Thinking Machines 本身使用了包括中国 Kimi K2.5 在内的模型作为 Inkling 的合成训练数据。

Nous 对 Qwen3.8-27B 进行了两个时期内约 5300 万个代币的监督微调训练，没有强化学习或偏好优化。该团队表示，他们事先消除了训练和测试提示之间的重叠。

Arete-27B 的事实准确性得分为 2.98，宣传性答案的比例下降至 0.9%。最大的转变出现在言论自由类别，事实得分从 0.89 跃升至 2.44，宣传率从 60% 下降至 1%。打开推理模式后，Arete 达到 3.07，尽管该数字仅基于迄今为止五次运行中的两次。

根据诺斯的说法，一般能力不会受到影响。在公司内部的 Hermes Bench 上，Arete-27B 的效率达到 65.60%，而基础型号的效率为 65.77%。在 Terminal-Bench 2.1 上，分数从 67% 上升到 70%，但 Nous 并不认为这是真正的进步，因为测试设置不同。

该团队的结论是“中国模型中的偏见层很浅”。该公司写道：“它应用得很晚，应用得很薄，经过精心挑选的监督的五千万代币可以将其移除，而不会干扰下面的任何东西。”

在《Arete》中，Nous 正朝着与《Hermes 3》不同的方向前进，《Hermes 3》在 2024 年故意保持中立，旨在适应系统提示中设置的任何世界观。中国模式的偏见是有据可查的。 2025 年，NewsGuard 发现，包括 Qwen 在内的 5 个领先模型在 60% 的案例中重复或未能纠正亲华虚假信息。

CrowdStrike 发现，当查询引用法轮功、西藏或台湾时，DeepSeek 会生成不太安全的代码。 Aleph Alpha 对 967 个政治敏感问题的研究得出了类似的结论：在阿里巴巴、DeepSeek 和 Moonshot AI 的模型中，只有 17% 到 41% 的答案是平衡的。

ValsAI 最近的一项研究还表明，并非所有中国模型的行为方式都相同：GLM-5.3 Flash 明确证实了侵犯人权行为，而 Kimi K3 否认了拘留营的存在。语言和回应格式对结果有明显影响，甚至西方模式也偶尔采用北京官方立场。事实证明，有针对性的微调也很有帮助。

Nous Research 在 10 月份的 B 轮融资中筹集了 9000 万美元，估值为 15 亿美元。 Robot Ventures 领投此轮融资，参与者包括英伟达 (Nvidia) 和三星 (Samsung)。 Nous 正在利用这笔资金通过“Hermes for Businesses”进入企业销售领域。 Arete-27B 的权重、测试数据集和训练数据可在 Hugging Face 上的 Apache 2.0 许可证下获取。

items.title: Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers
items.title_en: Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers
items.author: The Verge AI
items.article_content:
Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company's models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down.

That's according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation inside the company, as part of a report evaluating its AI research and development. The probe is separate from a program offering safety researchers "employee-like" access to systems in the wake of high-profile hacking incidents over the summer.

The findings offer some of the clearest evidence yet of AI …

items.title: Nine AI agents tried autonomous research on open questions from US national labs and none passed the experts' bar
items.title_en: Nine AI agents tried autonomous research on open questions from US national labs and none passed the experts' bar
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
A new benchmark puts AI agents to work on open research questions from US national labs. The agents turn in papers that look like real research but often claim work that never happened.

Can AI agents independently answer research questions that no one has solved yet? A team led by researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, working with scientists from US Department of Energy national labs, built a benchmark called "Into the Unknown" to find out.

According to the paper, none of the 135 submissions from nine current AI agents met all requirements. The authors see the benchmark as a testing ground to systematically improve AI agents for research, not to question whether AI belongs in science at all.

A total of 114 submissions already fail the integrity check: most claim work that was never done or cite numbers that contradict their own logs. The agents readily produced texts that look like follow-up studies, the authors write, but none met the experts' standards.

[caption id="attachment_63664" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] Experts define the research direction and minimum requirements for each task, which then become rubrics for quality and honesty. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

Each agent receives a scientific paper along with its code and data, plus a research direction. Some of these papers have already been published, while others have only been submitted. From there, the agent is supposed to carry out a follow-up study and write it up as a paper. The 15 tasks come from ten researchers across quantum computing, plasma physics, chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning. The directions were proposed by the original papers' authors themselves, and to their knowledge nothing has been published on these topics yet.

[caption id="attachment_63666" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] Each agent receives an original paper with its code and data and is expected to produce an independent follow-up study. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

Open research poses a basic problem: there's no answer key. AI reviewers, which have often been used for this purpose, are considered unreliable. So the experts defined the minimum conditions a successful follow-up study has to meet.

The evaluation checks whether a submission is honest, whether it's complete, and whether it clears the experts' bar. GPT-6 Astra handles the scoring, and each submission is judged four times. The agents tested were Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Deepseek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3. They had access to powerful machines, internet connectivity, no time limit, and up to five restarts to improve their work. In total, they ran for nearly 2,000 hours.

Only three agents produce honest work at all

Just three agents managed submissions without integrity violations: GPT-6 Astra on 11 of 15 tasks, GPT-5.6 Sol on six, and Claude Opus 5.5 on four. Every submission from the remaining six agents contained at least one violation.

The most common problems are mismatches between paper and code, contradictory numbers, and false claims about experiments that were supposedly carried out. Misreported baseline values pile up among the open models Deepseek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3. Two submissions with hardcoded rather than computed results came from Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3.

[caption id="attachment_63667" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] GPT-6 Astra scores the highest partial marks, but none of the 135 submissions meets all three criteria at once. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

Only one submission is complete, and it came from GPT-6 Astra. Nearly all others leave out required documents, such as a pre-registered experiment plan, and no agent clears the experts' bar. Under a more lenient scoring that accepts 90 percent of the rubric items, GPT-6 Astra comes closest, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol. The open models perform considerably worse overall.

[caption id="attachment_63670" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] Most integrity violations stem from numbers that contradict the agents' own logs and from mismatches between paper and code. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

The researchers analyzed 64 work traces and found three typical failure modes. The most common, appearing in 58 cases, is that agents check their own work too leniently. In 34 cases, agents spot a problem but document it instead of fixing it. In 21 cases, they unilaterally shrink the scope of the task.

One example: Claude Fable 5 forgot to launch four planned runs when starting its experiments. Its verification script adopted that same incomplete list and reported "4" runs completed. The agent trusted that result until the very end. In a different task, GPT-5.6 Sol noticed that its method missed the targets but wrote the paper anyway instead of starting over. DeepSeek V4 Pro dropped experiments because they were supposedly too slow for the "remaining time budget," even though there was no time limit.

[caption id="attachment_63663" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] Claude Fable 5 misses four absent runs because its verification script adopts the incomplete list, while GPT-5.6 Sol writes the paper despite missing its targets. | Image: Kim et al[/caption]

There are counterexamples, too: in a quantum task, GPT-5.6 Sol caught a fundamental error, stopped the running experiments, and recomputed everything from scratch.

Longer runtimes didn't lead to better results. DeepSeek V4 Pro and GLM-5.3 ran the longest at median times of 19.5 and 13.9 hours but scored poorly. GPT-6 Astra got by with a median of just 1.3 hours and delivered the best results.

[caption id="attachment_42539" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] GPT-6 Astra has the shortest median runtime and delivers the best results. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

Because the strongest model also served as the evaluator, the researchers ran a cross-check: the original papers' authors judged anonymized AI papers themselves. On whether a paper matched the given research direction, the automated system agreed with the experts in every case.

Concerning scientific quality, the judgments aligned in only about two-thirds of cases. One expert criticized, for instance, that the papers didn't tell a story. Judgments like these remain the job of human reviewers, the authors say.

The study's code and data are publicly available, and the project page hosts a leaderboard of the tested models.

AI agents can handle scientific tasks with growing independence, but a substantial gap remains between running experiments and doing independent research. A study from August already showed how much AI agents struggle with unpublished research questions. Epoch AI and Anthropic recently found that agents tend to present their results too favorably and don't sufficiently question failed approaches.

The picture looks much better for well-defined tasks: GPT-6 Astra solved 49 out of 50 unpublished problems in theoretical physics, though those solutions could be verified unambiguously. An analysis of more than 700 tasks from AI development also showed that while agents take on more and more practical work, humans still make the key research decisions.

Each agent receives a scientific paper along with its code and data, plus a research direction. Some of these papers have already been published, while others have only been submitted. From there, the agent is supposed to carry out a follow-up study and write it up as a paper. The 15 tasks come from ten researchers across quantum computing, plasma physics, chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning. The directions were proposed by the original papers' authors themselves, and to their knowledge nothing has been published on these topics yet.

[caption id="attachment_63666" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] Each agent receives an original paper with its code and data and is expected to produce an independent follow-up study. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

Open research poses a basic problem: there's no answer key. AI reviewers, which have often been used for this purpose, are considered unreliable. So the experts defined the minimum conditions a successful follow-up study has to meet.

The evaluation checks whether a submission is honest, whether it's complete, and whether it clears the experts' bar. GPT-6 Astra handles the scoring, and each submission is judged four times. The agents tested were Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Deepseek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3. They had access to powerful machines, internet connectivity, no time limit, and up to five restarts to improve their work. In total, they ran for nearly 2,000 hours.

Only three agents produce honest work at all

Just three agents managed submissions without integrity violations: GPT-6 Astra on 11 of 15 tasks, GPT-5.6 Sol on six, and Claude Opus 5.5 on four. Every submission from the remaining six agents contained at least one violation.

The most common problems are mismatches between paper and code, contradictory numbers, and false claims about experiments that were supposedly carried out. Misreported baseline values pile up among the open models Deepseek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3. Two submissions with hardcoded rather than computed results came from Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3.

[caption id="attachment_63667" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] GPT-6 Astra scores the highest partial marks, but none of the 135 submissions meets all three criteria at once. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

Only one submission is complete, and it came from GPT-6 Astra. Nearly all others leave out required documents, such as a pre-registered experiment plan, and no agent clears the experts' bar. Under a more lenient scoring that accepts 90 percent of the rubric items, GPT-6 Astra comes closest, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol. The open models perform considerably worse overall.

[caption id="attachment_63670" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] Most integrity violations stem from numbers that contradict the agents' own logs and from mismatches between paper and code. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

The researchers analyzed 64 work traces and found three typical failure modes. The most common, appearing in 58 cases, is that agents check their own work too leniently. In 34 cases, agents spot a problem but document it instead of fixing it. In 21 cases, they unilaterally shrink the scope of the task.

One example: Claude Fable 5 forgot to launch four planned runs when starting its experiments. Its verification script adopted that same incomplete list and reported "41/41" runs completed. The agent trusted that result until the very end. In a different task, GPT-5.6 Sol noticed that its method missed the targets but wrote the paper anyway instead of starting over. DeepSeek V4 Pro dropped experiments because they were supposedly too slow for the "remaining time budget," even though there was no time limit.

[caption id="attachment_63663" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] Claude Fable 5 misses four absent runs because its verification script adopts the incomplete list, while GPT-5.6 Sol writes the paper despite missing its targets. | Image: Kim et al[/caption]

There are counterexamples, too: in a quantum task, GPT-5.6 Sol caught a fundamental error, stopped the running experiments, and recomputed everything from scratch.

Longer runtimes didn't lead to better results. DeepSeek V4 Pro and GLM-5.3 ran the longest at median times of 19.5 and 13.9 hours but scored poorly. GPT-6 Astra got by with a median of just 1.3 hours and delivered the best results.

[caption id="attachment_42539" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] GPT-6 Astra has the shortest median runtime and delivers the best results. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

Because the strongest model also served as the evaluator, the researchers ran a cross-check: the original papers' authors judged anonymized AI papers themselves. On whether a paper matched the given research direction, the automated system agreed with the experts in every case.

Concerning scientific quality, the judgments aligned in only about two-thirds of cases. One expert criticized, for instance, that the papers didn't tell a story. Judgments like these remain the job of human reviewers, the authors say.

The study's code and data are publicly available, and the project page hosts a leaderboard of the tested models.

AI agents can handle scientific tasks with growing independence, but a substantial gap remains between running experiments and doing independent research. A study from August already showed how much AI agents struggle with unpublished research questions. Epoch AI and Anthropic recently found that agents tend to present their results too favorably and don't sufficiently question failed approaches.

The picture looks much better for well-defined tasks: GPT-6 Astra solved 49 out of 50 unpublished problems in theoretical physics, though those solutions could be verified unambiguously. An analysis of more than 700 tasks from AI development also showed that while agents take on more and more practical work, humans still make the key research decisions.

items.article_content_zh:
一项新的基准让人工智能代理致力于解决美国国家实验室的开放研究问题。特工们提交的论文看起来像是真正的研究，但往往声称他们的工作从未发生过。

人工智能代理能否独立回答尚未解决的研究问题？由卡内基梅隆大学研究人员领导的一个团队与美国能源部国家实验室的科学家合作，建立了一个名为“进入未知”的基准来找出答案。

根据该论文，当前 9 名 AI 代理提交的 135 份材料均未满足所有要求。作者将该基准视为系统地改进用于研究的人工智能代理的试验场，而不是质疑人工智能是否属于科学。

总共 114 份提交的内容已经未能通过完整性检查：大多数声称工作从未完成，或者引用了与自己的日志相矛盾的数字。作者写道，特工们很容易制作出看起来像是后续研究的文本，但没有一个符合专家的标准。

专家定义每项任务的研究方向和最低要求，然后这些成为质量和诚实的准则。 |图片：Kim 等人[/标题]

每个代理都会收到一篇科学论文及其代码和数据，以及一个研究方向。其中一些论文已经发表，而另一些则刚刚提交。从那里，代理应该进行后续研究并将其写成论文。这 15 项任务来自量子计算、等离子体物理、化学、材料科学和科学机器学习领域的 10 名研究人员。这些方向是由原始论文作者自己提出的，据他们所知，尚未就这些主题发表任何内容。

每个代理都会收到一份包含代码和数据的原始论文，并预计将产生独立的后续研究。 |图片：Kim 等人[/标题]

开放研究提出了一个基本问题：没有答案。经常用于此目的的人工智能评审员被认为是不可靠的。因此，专家们定义了成功的后续研究必须满足的最低条件。

评估会检查提交的内容是否诚实、是否完整以及是否通过了专家的审核。 GPT-6 Astra 负责评分，每份提交作品都会被评判四次。测试的代理包括 Claude Opus 4.8、Claude Opus 5、Claude Fable 5、Claude Opus 5.5、GPT-5.6 Sol、GPT-6 Astra、Deepseek V4 Pro、Kimi K3 和 GLM-5.3。他们可以使用功能强大的机器、互联网连接、没有时间限制，并且最多可以重新启动五次来改进他们的工作。他们总共运行了近 2,000 小时。

只有三个代理人能够诚实地工作

只有三个代理管理了没有完整性违规的提交：GPT-6 Astra 完成了 15 项任务中的 11 项，GPT-5.6 Sol 完成了 6 项任务，Claude Opus 5.5 完成了 4 项任务。其余六名特工提交的每份材料都至少包含一项违规行为。

最常见的问题是纸张和代码之间的不匹配、相互矛盾的数字以及对本应进行的实验的虚假陈述。开放模型 Deepseek V4 Pro、Kimi K3 和 GLM-5.3 中错误报告的基线值堆积如山。 Kimi K3 和 GLM-5.3 提交了两份具有硬编码结果而非计算结果的提交。

GPT-6 Astra 获得了最高的部分分数，但 135 份提交的作品中没有一个同时满足所有三个标准。 |图片：Kim 等人[/标题]

只有一份提交是完整的，它来自 GPT-6 Astra。几乎所有其他人都遗漏了所需的文件，例如预先注册的实验计划，并且没有代理人通过专家栏。在接受 90% 的评分标准的更宽松的评分下，GPT-6 Astra 最接近，其次是 Claude Opus 5.5 和 GPT-5.6 Sol。开放模型的整体表现要差得多。

【起因与机理】AI代理在复杂科研场景中表现出严重的幻觉与诚信缺失
【关键技术规格】AI智能体在科研基准测试中全部失败。
【观点态度】证明AI尚不具备独立处理复杂科研的能力。

[Root Cause & Mechanism] AI agents exhibit hallucinations and lack of academic integrity in research
[Key Specification] AI agents failed all scientific benchmarks.
[Perspective & Impact] Proving current AI cannot handle independent complex research.

items.title: Apps for Caregivers Get a Dose of AI, but That Might Not Be Enough
items.title_en: Apps for Caregivers Get a Dose of AI, but That Might Not Be Enough
items.author: Wired AI
items.article_content:
We’re not alone in our struggles. According to AARP, in 2025, an estimated 63 million Americans cared for adults or children with a medical condition or disability. On average, these caregivers spend up to 27 hours per week providing care.

This caregiver crisis, where so many Americans provide ongoing, complex care and, as a result, endure poor health, financial strain, and isolation, is worsening as caregivers need more support and better systems.

Helpfully, to lighten the mental load, caregiver apps are aimed at families who are supporting seniors, children, or anyone with a diagnosis that needs regular management.

Every caregiver’s situation is different, and the apps and programs in this space reflect a diversity of needs.

Medisafe, which was created in 2013, tracks medications and sends reminders so users don’t miss a dose. The program can also notify a caregiver if a dose is missed. It gives its users the ability to track medical appointments, track their symptoms, and maintain a list of health care contacts and measurements. It also has a drug interaction checker where users can enter multiple medications to see if they are safe to take at the same time.

Caring Village, which was founded in 2015, has an appointment calendar, a to-do list, and a wellness journal where users can keep track of their loved one’s symptoms and moods, and even upload a photo. Caregivers can assign tasks through the app, create a care plan, and receive reminders to take medication. The app also comes with an AI assistant called Julia that can answer caregiving questions.

In 2022, Bret Koncak, based on his experiences with his two sons who have complex needs, cocreated Mejo, a web-based caregiver app. Users enter an individual’s medical history, which is then consolidated into a one-page summary that can be shared with caregivers, doctors, and therapists.

“A lot of people think that caregiving begins and ends with interactions with the health care system, but a lot of it is about what happens between care visits,” says Koncak. “That's what we're focused on.” For $6 a month or $60 a year, the premium version of Mejo gives users access to daily journaling, which they can share with other caregivers, so everyone stays on the same page without having to catch up verbally.

For now, information in Mejo is entered manually, but Koncak says his team is looking into ways to incorporate AI to help users come up with appropriate questions to ask during medical appointments.

Brett Rowell, whose son Briggs has cerebral palsy, is creating an app called Briggzy, so he and his wife, who work different hours, can more easily hand off their son’s care. Briggzy is currently in the testing phase, and Rowell hopes to launch it to a wider community in 2027.

“My wife took [our son] to most of the appointments because I worked 8 to 5 and she was off during that time,” said Rowell. “So the questionnaires alone, I don't know how to answer half of them unless I have Briggzy. My goal was to bring her mind into a shared space for me, so that way I can be helpful.”

Nasha Fitter, who has a daughter with a rare disease, launched Citizen Health in 2024 with cofounder Farid Vij to collect medical records for patients and store them in a secure portal. “With the users’ consent, we can extract information from those medical records, deidentify it, harmonize it, and start to pull an understanding of diseases through that,” says Fitter. “And then we feed that understanding back to patients so they would get a better sense of the trajectory of their child’s disease.” Citizen Health works with patient advocacy groups to support their research on drug development.

Six months ago, the company launched Ari, an AI “health teammate” that lets caregivers and patients track their loved one's care and symptoms by texting with it. Ari, currently in beta, can also access medical records, patient portals, and Google Calendar events, including specific appointment dates and surgeries. Ari notices caregiver patterns, such as whether they take medication at different times of the day and how that might impact symptoms. It prepares patients and caregivers for appointments by summarizing past medical information and providing appropriate questions to ask medical professionals. And it can help navigate insurance and government benefits.

Right now, Ari is only available for people with rare diseases, but the goal is to make it available and useful to all caregivers and patients.

I. Glenn Cohen, a bioethics and health law researcher and professor at Harvard Law School, is optimistic about AI in the health space overall. “For example, I think it will empower many patients to prep for questions they might want to ask their doctor before going in to see them.”

But he says that users should go into the process with their eyes open to understand the risks and what you're getting out of it, especially if a product is free or cheap.

Most of these devices are not medical devices, says Cohen. “As such, the FDA has not reviewed them, so their safety and efficacy remain a question mark, or it's the company's word for it that you have to take.”

The health information patients and caregivers plug into these AI tools is not protected by federal HIPAA statutes because the information is typically not coming from a covered entity. Instead, it comes from a person or from data collection at home. “If your privacy is important and you care about how the information is used, in some cases, all you can rely on is the contractual promises,” Cohen says. “They typically have language that absolves [the companies] from responsibility in many instances.”

He also warns that the information collected may not be only for the person receiving care, but may also include information about parents or other caregivers.

While I love the idea of keeping my son’s information all in one place so I can keep track of patterns, update his doctors without feeling emotionally drained, and easily hand off his caregiving needs to my husband, making sure we update the app regularly will be the key to actually seeing those benefits.

Denise M. Brown, CEO and founder of the Caregiving Years Training Academy, has seen many apps come and go because she says they can be tedious to maintain, especially when caregivers are already overloaded.

“We have to upload data to the app (care plans, schedules, tasks), and that’s a lot of work,” Brown says. “A physician, visiting nurse, therapist, or hospital discharge planner won’t log into the app to provide updates, which ends up falling back on the caregiver.”

At the end of the day, the need for caregiver apps is great, and many developers in this community, many of whom are caregivers themselves, are trying to do something to lessen the load.

“The technology and apps can open the door for broader seamless integration of care—and hopefully less stress on you as the caregiver,” says Nicole Howell, director of direct care workforce development at the National Council on Aging. But she says the final solution [to the overall caregiver crisis] will be something that not one family, not one caregiver can solve.

“It has to be all hands at the wheel. It has to be government. It has to be private. It has to be family members speaking up, saying the hard truth so we get the best of American ingenuity to move this to where we need to be.”

items.article_content_zh:
我们并不孤单地在挣扎。据 AARP 称，到 2025 年，估计有 6300 万美国人需要照顾患有疾病或残疾的成人或儿童。这些护理人员平均每周花费长达 27 个小时提供护理。

由于护理人员需要更多的支持和更好的系统，许多美国人提供持续、复杂的护理，因此面临健康状况不佳、经济紧张和孤立的情况，这场护理人员危机正在恶化。

有益的是，为了减轻精神负担，看护应用程序针对的是支持老年人、儿童或任何患有需要定期管理的诊断的人的家庭。

每个护理人员的情况都不同，这个领域的应用程序和程序反映了多样化的需求。

Medisafe 于 2013 年创建，可跟踪药物并发送提醒，以便用户不会错过服药。如果错过剂量，该程序还可以通知护理人员。它使用户能够跟踪医疗预约、跟踪他们的症状并维护医疗保健联系人和测量结果的列表。它还具有药物相互作用检查器，用户可以输入多种药物，看看同时服用它们是否安全。

Caring Village 成立于 2015 年，提供预约日历、待办事项列表和健康日记，用户可以在其中跟踪亲人的症状和情绪，甚至上传照片。护理人员可以通过应用程序分配任务、制定护理计划并接收服药提醒。该应用程序还配备了一个名为 Julia 的人工智能助手，可以回答护理问题。

2022 年，Bret Koncak 根据他与两个有着复杂需求的儿子的经历，共同创建了 Mejo，一款基于网络的护理应用程序。用户输入个人的病史，然后将其合并为一页摘要，可以与护理人员、医生和治疗师共享。

“很多人认为护理的开始和结束都是与医疗保健系统的互动，但其中很多是关于护理访问之间发生的事情，”Koncak 说。 “这就是我们关注的重点。”每月 6 美元或每年 60 美元，Mejo 的高级版本让用户可以访问每日日记，他们可以与其他护理人员分享这些日记，这样每个人都可以保持在同一页面上，而无需口头交流。

目前，Mejo 中的信息是手动输入的，但 Koncak 表示，他的团队正在研究如何整合人工智能，以帮助用户在医疗预约期间提出适当的问题。

Brett Rowell 的儿子 Briggs 患有脑瘫，他正在开发一款名为 Briggzy 的应用程序，这样他和工作时间不同的妻子就可以更轻松地照顾儿子。 Briggzy 目前正处于测试阶段，Rowell 希望在 2027 年将其推出到更广泛的社区。

“我的妻子带着（我们的儿子）参加了大部分的预约，因为我朝八晚五工作，而她在那段时间休息，”罗威尔说。 “仅凭问卷调查，除非有 Briggzy，否则我不知道如何回答其中一半问题。我的目标是让她的思想与我共享空间，这样我就能提供帮助。”

Nasha Fitter 的女儿患有罕见疾病，她与联合创始人 Farid Vij 于 2024 年推出了 Citizen Health，收集患者的医疗记录并将其存储在安全门户中。 “在用户同意的情况下，我们可以从这些医疗记录中提取信息，对其进行去识别化、协调化，并开始通过这些信息了解疾病，”菲特说。 “然后我们将这种理解反馈给患者，以便他们更好地了解孩子的疾病轨迹。” Citizen Health 与患者倡导团体合作，支持他们的药物开发研究。

六个月前，该公司推出了人工智能“健康队友”Ari，让护理人员和患者可以通过发短信来跟踪亲人的护理和症状。目前处于测试阶段的 Ari 还可以访问医疗记录、患者门户和 Google 日历事件，包括特定的预约日期和手术。阿里注意到护理人员的模式，例如他们是否在一天的不同时间服药以及这可能如何影响症状。它通过总结过去的医疗信息并提供适当的问题来询问医疗专业人员，为患者和护理人员的预约做好准备。它还可以帮助了解保险和政府福利。

目前，Ari 仅适用于患有罕见疾病的人，但目标是使其对所有护理人员和患者都可用且有用。

items.title: Google's AI detects high blood pressure from a regular smartwatch without a cuff
items.title_en: Google's AI detects high blood pressure from a regular smartwatch without a cuff
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
A Google Research AI can detect signs of high blood pressure using a regular smartwatch, with no blood pressure cuff needed for calibration. The AI relies on two sensors already built into modern watches—a pulse sensor and a motion sensor—according to a Google blog post. The study was published in Nature.

A neural network learned from nearly 500,000 hours of sensor data by comparing short segments and figuring out which ones belonged to the same person, picking up typical pulse and heartbeat patterns without any diagnoses to guide it. The system then averages these patterns over several days and calculates a probability for high blood pressure. Google's health model SensorFM also learns from smartwatch data.

In a study of 196 people across five US research sites, the watch spotted hypertension about as well as a traditional cuff, identifying 65.8 percent of those with high blood pressure compared to 55.3 percent for the standard in-office measurement.

Google says the findings have been folded into the blood pressure trends feature in the Google Health app, but the method is still a research project and doesn't replace a diagnosis. The goal is to nudge people toward getting checked. More than half of people with high blood pressure don't know they have it, according to Google.

items.article_content_zh:
谷歌研究人工智能可以使用普通智能手表检测高血压迹象，无需血压袖带进行校准。根据谷歌博客文章，人工智能依赖于现代手表中内置的两个传感器——脉冲传感器和运动传感器。该研究发表在《自然》杂志上。

神经网络通过比较短片段并找出哪些片段属于同一个人，从近 500,000 小时的传感器数据中学习，在没有任何诊断指导的情况下获取典型的脉搏和心跳模式。然后，系统对几天内的这些模式进行平均，并计算出高血压的概率。谷歌的健康模型 SensorFM 也可以从智能手表数据中学习。

在一项针对美国 5 个研究中心 196 人的研究中，这款手表发现高血压的效果与传统袖带的效果相当，识别出 65.8% 的高血压患者，而标准办公室测量的识别率为 55.3%。

谷歌表示，这些发现已被纳入谷歌健康应用程序的血压趋势功能中，但该方法仍然是一个研究项目，并不能取代诊断。目标是促使人们接受检查。据谷歌称，超过一半的高血压患者并不知道自己患有高血压。

items.title: OpenAI lands an $11 billion funding round, but has to court dentists for more capital
items.title_en: OpenAI lands an $11 billion funding round, but has to court dentists for more capital
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
OpenAI has received roughly $11 billion in new funding, the first tranche of a round valuing the company at $1.25 trillion. The money was wired on Friday, Bloomberg reports. The full round could grow to $20 billion, with the rest expected in the coming weeks. OpenAI originally sought $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation but scaled back after an AI-sector selloff. Anthropic's valuation is also under pressure ahead of its planned IPO.

Investors include Coatue Management, T. Rowe Price, SoftBank, Sequoia Capital, Founders Fund, Andreessen Horowitz, and a consortium from the United Arab Emirates. OpenAI is also working with investment banks to bring in wealthy individual investors. If OpenAI is already courting dentists to scrape together more capital, it tells you the AI funding market is either tapped out or too concentrated on OpenAI and Anthropic. Anthropic's massive B2B success with Claude Code is making life even harder for OpenAI.

items.article_content_zh:
OpenAI 已获得约 110 亿美元的新融资，这是该公司估值 1.25 万亿美元的第一轮融资。据彭博社报道，这笔钱已于周五汇出。整轮融资可能会增至 200 亿美元，其余预计将在未来几周内完成。 OpenAI 最初以 1.4 万亿美元的估值寻求 300 亿美元的融资，但在人工智能行业遭遇抛售后缩减了规模。在计划首次公开募股之前，Anthropic 的估值也面临压力。

投资者包括 Coatue Management、T. Rowe Price、软银、红杉资本、Founders Fund、Andreessen Horowitz 以及来自阿拉伯联合酋长国的财团。 OpenAI 还与投资银行合作，引进富有的个人投资者。如果 OpenAI 已经在吸引牙医筹集更多资金，那么这说明人工智能融资市场要么已经被耗尽，要么过于集中于 OpenAI 和 Anthropic。 Anthropic 凭借 Claude Code 在 B2B 领域取得的巨大成功让 OpenAI 的日子变得更加艰难。

【起因与机理】AI行业融资环境收紧，迫使公司不得不下调预期并扩大募资对象
【关键数据与实测】OpenAI达成110亿美元初期融资。
【观点态度】募资渠道下沉至高净值个人。

[Root Cause & Mechanism] Tightening AI capital markets forcing valuation cuts and broadened investor search
[Key Metrics] OpenAI hits $11B in initial funding.
[Perspective & Impact] Capital sourcing extended to high-net-worth individuals.

items.title: Global tablet shipments fell 23% YoY to 32M units in Q3 2026, their lowest level in nearly three years; Apple's iPad shipments fell 27.5% YoY to ~11.58M (Omdia)
items.title_en: Global tablet shipments fell 23% YoY to 32M units in Q3 2026, their lowest level in nearly three years; Apple's iPad shipments fell 27.5% YoY to ~11.58M (Omdia)
items.author: Omdia
items.article_content:
LONDON, November 5, 2026: The global tablet market fell 23% year-over-year (YoY) to 32 million units in Q3 2026, marking its lowest shipment level in nearly three years, according to Omdia’s latest research. The Middle East, China and Western Europe were the hardest-hit regions, experiencing sharper declines than the rest of the market.

"Following a 10% decline last quarter, the tablet market recorded another double-digit contraction in Q3," said Himani Mukka, Research Manager at Omdia. "As supply constraints intensify, tablets are increasingly taking a backseat in vendors' strategic priorities for 2026 and 2027. With supply conditions expected to tighten further next year, a meaningful recovery in the tablet market is unlikely before 2028.”

In 3Q26, Apple maintained its lead despite a 28% YoY decline in shipments. Its market share fell to 36% from 38.2% a year earlier, as its shipments declined more sharply than the overall market.

Samsung remained in second place, shipping 5.4 million units, down 22 % YoY, and capturing a 16.9% market share. Despite new tablet launches, the company continued to face pressure as component constraints weighed on shipment volumes.

As in Q2, Lenovo was the only top-five vendor to post growth, with shipments increasing 12% YoY to 4.1 million units. Its market share climbed to 12.7%, up from 8.7% a year earlier, marking the largest share increase among vendors this quarter. While detachable shipments declined sharply year on year, slate tablets drove overall growth, supported by stronger sell-in across all regions except Europe and Latin America.

Xiaomi ranked fourth, shipping 2.3 million tablets, down 11% year on year. Its market share rose modestly to 7.3%, supported by a strong quarter in Latin America. Huawei rounded out the top five with 1.8 million units, recording the steepest decline among the leading vendors at 43% year on year. Despite the overall downturn, the vendor continued to register growth in CEE and APAC this quarter.

Mukka added,“We have seen several major tablet launches in the back half of the year, including Samsung's flagship Galaxy Tab S12 series, Apple's OLED-equipped iPad mini, and Xiaomi's Pad 9 series. Huawei, HONOR, OnePlus and realme have also introduced new models recently. However, these launches have done little to stimulate consumer demand amid challenging market conditions.”

“Persistent supply constraints are also limiting vendors' ability to deliver meaningful specification upgrades, leaving fewer compelling differences between new models and their predecessors. As a result, consumers are increasingly expected to delay purchases until more substantial improvements become available.”

items.article_content_zh:
伦敦，2026 年 11 月 5 日：根据 Omdia 的最新研究，2026 年第三季度全球平板电脑市场同比下降 23%，至 3200 万台，创下近三年来的最低出货量。中东、中国和西欧是受灾最严重的地区，其跌幅比市场其他地区更严重。

Omdia 研究经理 Himani Mukka 表示：“继上季度下滑 10% 后，平板电脑市场在第三季度再次出现两位数萎缩。” “随着供应限制的加剧，平板电脑在供应商 2026 年和 2027 年的战略重点中日益退居次席。由于明年供应状况预计将进一步收紧，平板电脑市场在 2028 年之前不太可能出现有意义的复苏。”

26 年第三季度，尽管苹果出货量同比下降 28%，但仍保持领先地位。由于出货量下降幅度超过整体市场，其市场份额从去年同期的 38.2% 下降至 36%。

三星仍位居第二，出货量为 540 万台，同比下降 22%，占据 16.9% 的市场份额。尽管推出了新的平板电脑，但由于组件限制影响了出货量，该公司继续面临压力。

与第二季度一样，联想是前五名中唯一实现增长的厂商，出货量同比增长 12% 至 410 万台。其市场份额从去年同期的8.7%攀升至12.7%，是本季度厂商中份额增幅最大的。尽管可拆卸出货量同比大幅下降，但在除欧洲和拉丁美洲以外的所有地区销售强劲的支撑下，平板电脑推动了整体增长。

小米排名第四，平板电脑出货量为230万台，同比下降11%。在拉丁美洲强劲季度的支撑下，其市场份额小幅上升至 7.3%。华为以 180 万台跻身前五，同比下降 43%，是领先厂商中跌幅最大的。尽管整体低迷，该供应商本季度在中东欧和亚太地区继续实现增长。

Mukka补充道：“今年下半年，我们看到了几款主要的平板电脑发布，包括三星旗舰产品Galaxy Tab S12系列、苹果配备OLED的iPad mini和小米Pad 9系列。华为、荣耀、一加和realme最近也推出了新机型。然而，在充满挑战的市场条件下，这些发布对刺激消费者需求作用甚微。”

“持续的供应限制也限制了供应商提供有意义的规格升级的能力，从而使新型号与其前身之间的显着差异减少。因此，越来越多的消费者预计会推迟购买，直到出现更多实质性改进。”

items.summary_en: Shenzhen is clearing out illicit electronics markets like Huaqiangbei, specifically targeting the smuggling of chips and stolen iPhone trade. The action aims to clean up the industry environment ahead of the upcoming APEC summit.
items.title_zh: 深圳清理电子黑市迎峰会
items.summary_zh: 深圳在APEC峰会前夕整顿华强北等电子市场，重点打击芯片走私及翻新机交易，规范电子产业链环境

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 深圳近日对华强北等电子产品聚集区展开清理行动，针对非法芯片贸易与盗窃翻新手机市场进行打击。此举旨在改善国际峰会前的城市形象与行业秩序，试图将野蛮生长的灰色产业纳入监管视线。

items.title: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO
items.title_en: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO
items.author: The Verge AI
items.article_content:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

CEO Sam Altman said recently that OpenAI is prioritizing safety instead of going ‘guns blazing’ toward an IPO.﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI is now valued at $1.25 trillion in a new round of funding that has raised another $11 billion, according to Bloomberg. That would make it one of the world’s most valuable companies, not long after raising $122 billion from investors in March at a valuation of $852 billion.

Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion. That was before tech stocks dropped, and the results of the midterms showed how much public opinion has turned against AI companies and data center projects.

OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week. Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it’s holding off on its own IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models’ safety. He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

OpenAI 在新一轮融资中目前估值为 1.25 万亿美元，该轮融资又筹集了 110 亿美元。这将使其成为世界上最有价值的公司之一，不久之后，该公司于 3 月份以 8520 亿美元的估值从投资者那里筹集了 1220 亿美元。

彭博社回应《金融时报》和《华尔街日报》上周的报道称，OpenAI 仍在寻求额外投资，可能将融资金额增加至 200 亿美元，并且最初希望以 1.4 万亿美元的估值筹集至多 300 亿美元。那是在科技股下跌之前，中期选举的结果表明公众舆论已经转向反对人工智能公司和数据中心项目。

OpenAI 的竞争对手 Anthropic 上周提交了 S-1 上市申请。今年早些时候，OpenAI 首席执行官 Sam Altman 表示，公司将推迟 IPO，直到对其模型的安全性做出更有信心的声明。他没有给出 IPO 的具体时间表，但当时表示，“我认为，如果 OpenAI 等待太久才上市，对世界来说也是件坏事。”

items.title_zh: 苹果称iPhone Duo专用应用已破十万大关
items.summary_zh: 苹果宣布专为iPhone Duo设计的应用已超10万款，且每日新增数千款优化应用

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 苹果官方近期宣布，针对iPhone Duo开发的专用App Store应用数量已正式突破10万大关，并保持着每天数千款的增长速度。尽管已进行大规模适配，部分应用在双屏交互下的用户体验仍有待优化。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Apple officially announced that the App Store now features over 100,000 apps specifically designed for the iPhone Duo, with thousands more added daily. Despite the rapid growth in optimized software, user experience for some apps on the dual-screen form factor remains a work in progress.

elements_zh.where: App Store生态系统
elements_zh.what: 专用适配应用突破10万，并维持高速增长
elements_zh.why: 推动iPhone Duo双屏硬件的普及与生态适配

elements_en.what: Reached 100k+ dedicated apps with rapid daily additions
elements_en.why: To drive adoption and ecosystem support for iPhone Duo hardware

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 应用数量虽多，但这种为了填补屏幕缝隙而强行适配的操作，本质上还是在考验开发者“缝合”代码的耐心。毕竟用户买的是创新，不是一个比原来多装了十万个图标的折叠屏充电宝。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Hitting 100k apps is just a numbers game for PR; most users just want a seamless experience, not a glorified charging brick with a thousand redundant icons. It’s a classic case of 'if you build it, they will come'—eventually, maybe.

items.title_zh: 谷歌接盘Crusoe怀俄明州数据中心地块
items.summary_zh: 谷歌收购了Crusoe位于怀俄明州的数据中心项目地块，此前该项目未能吸引谷歌作为客户

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 谷歌正式收购了Crusoe位于怀俄明州东南部的土地资产。这一地块原为Crusoe筹建的数据中心项目，但由于该项目未能成功争取到谷歌等关键客户入驻，最终沦为被金主爸爸“反向收购”的资产。

elements_en.what: Google bought out Crusoe's data center site
elements_en.why: Crusoe failed to secure necessary anchor tenants like Google for its project

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 创业公司想靠建数据中心“空手套大厂”确实不容易，最后没能把云服务卖给谷歌，干脆把自己打包卖给谷歌了。这哪是商业合作，分明是一场“乙方变废纸、甲方直接收尸”的精准降维打击。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Attempting to trap big tech in a data center deal is a bold move that backfired spectacularly; when you can't sell them the cloud, you end up selling them your empty dirt. It’s a brutal reminder that in the AI arms race, if you aren't the landlord, you're just the furniture.

items.title: Chainalysis says hackers stole credentials and tokens for all of its customers
items.title_en: Chainalysis says hackers stole credentials and tokens for all of its customers
items.author: Ars Technica
items.article_content:
Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said that hackers have obtained sensitive personal information—including names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens—for all of its users following a breach of its network security.

The accomplishment could be a major coup for the attackers. Both Chainalysis and public sources have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It's unclear if the data theft exposed customers to additional threats.

Last Friday, Chainalysis said it had been the target of a cybersecurity incident in October that was similar to the hacks of other platforms during the same month. The external actor used AI agent-assisted offensive techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools. An email the company sent to affected customers said some “non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed.” It's not clear why the company considered such

items.title: All the latest updates on AI data centers
items.title_en: All the latest updates on AI data centers
items.author: The Verge AI
items.article_content:
Massive new data centers are the physical foundation for tech companies’ hopes and dreams for AI. But the rush to expand warehouses full of energy-hungry servers has also kicked up fights across the world over their impact on power grids, utility bills, nearby communities, and the environment.

Data centers were a major bipartisan issue ahead of the 2026 midterms, and voters largely opposed data center expansion at the polls. Tech giants like OpenAI and Amazon are promising to work more closely with local communities and cover their data center energy costs. But following the election, Democratic leaders are calling for further data center restrictions and slowdowns that the AI companies will have to grapple with.

From audacious plans about data centers into space, heated local battles over buildouts, and potential environmental impacts, here’s The Verge’s news, coverage, and reporting surrounding data centers and the companies that are building them.
